title: Idea: Could Deno be self-hosting someday?
body:
As we all know, Deno right now is written in Rust with several libraries like Tokio. But could the day ever come where Deno is self-hosting, as in the Deno source code is written in TypeScript and is turned into an executable using e.g. `deno compile`?

Deno's goal is to be a complete toolchain. If it does become self-hosting, then it joins C/C++ and Rust as one of the few toolchains powerful enough to not need to depend on anything except itself.

Advantages:
* **Completes the Circle of Life**: Becoming self-hosting or self-compiling is a big milestone for any language or project. It proves just how strong and mature your technology is. People started taking Rust and LLVM much more seriously once they were feature-complete enough to be used for building themselves.
* **Security**: Rust is safer, but it's not invincible. Unsafe code is still possible. If Deno ever becomes self-hosting enough to compile itself and all dependencies are written in TypeScript, then all code will be written in a language that doesn't allow low-level access to unsafe things like memory in the first place.
* **Package management at its finest**: Decentralized ES Modules for every dependency. No one single source or website to rely on for its building blocks.

Disadvantages:
* **Performance**: Deno right now has Rust and Tokio to provide as much performance as it needs. [NectarJS](https://github.com/NectarJS/nectarjs) proved that JavaScript can be compiled to native code without GC, but getting things like TCP working on at or near the same level as Rust would likely require quite a bit of time and effort. 
* **Cost of Refactoring**: Deno only became stable in May 2020. Adding new features is what the core team is focused on right now. Refactoring the codebase into TypeScript may not be something welcomed by the developers.

Does anyone have any thoughts? Are there any pros/cons I'm not thinking of? What does the Deno team think?

The feeling is it erodes security and it often used by people who don't understand the implications of what they are doing, and don't understand the right ways to address the issues they are encountering.

author: kitsonk

title: Design Meeting 2021-08-05
body:
- Update on `deno_graph`
  - was discussed the previous week as part of Q3 roadmap review, but @kitsonk gave a further update on progress, well on track.
  - Discussion about whether import map should be pulled into `deno_graph` or not, as those consuming it would want to have support for import maps.  The functionality is abstracted out as the `Resolver` trait, but there is no implementation.
  - Decision was to wait until the integration of `deno_graph` into CLI occurs.
  - Next step was integration into `deno_doc`.
- Service Workers, do we actually need them? (#5957)
  - Discussion around what they are actually good for as part of Deno.  There is no compelling use case that they solve, and to implement compliant service workers is complicated and full of challenges that would need to be solved.
  - Note, this does not mean that the `Cache` and `CacheStorage` APIs are un-needed or unwanted.  They were implemented as part of service workers and are critical to service workers, but they aren't isolated to service workers in the web platform.
  - _Decision_ the core team is not opposed to service workers, but there is no compelling use case we can see. If someone had a use case and wanted to contribute it to Deno we wouldn't oppose it, though we caution any implementors that _there be dragons_.
- Quota Management and StorageManager API (https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/11525)
  - Discussed that all browsers have a non-user facing quota manager.  How they implement it varies from browser to browser.
  - Quota Management is an internal API that enables other user facing features.  The StorageManager API gives a user some view into storage and capacity management to better manage their workloads.
  - Discussed that `DENO_DIR` is unbounded in size and we need to do something eventually there.
  - There is nothing _currently broken_ that this would fix, but if we were to add `CacheStorage` or `IndexedDB` it starts to become a problem.
  - @ry concerned about expending effort on something that doesn't actually fix anything that is broken or doesn't deliver a direct user feature.  Is this pre-mature optimisation?
  - _Action_ to have a breakout meeting once people have better context and have done more research.
- Plan for deprecating `std/http` and `std/ws` (https://github.com/denoland/deno_std/discussions/1034)
  - @kitsonk is concerned that the proposal is just another abstraction and API we have to support.  It isn't compatible with `std/http` as it exists.
  - It is trivial to implement.
  - @ry wondered what would happen with oak since native HTTP was stabilised, @kitsonk indicated it would just start using native.
  - _Action_ determine how someone would change a `std/http` application to work with the new `std` abstraction. If it is change a couple lines, great, if it is more complicated, what value does a new abstraction bring?
- Enable Deno APIs by default in Workers (#8178)
  - Ultimately it is a _mistake_ we made with 1.0.
  - It was not until Deno 1.4 that workers could access the `Deno` namespace and only with an explicit flag.
  - Changing it before 2.0 is likely to cause strange and exotic regressions in code, because of the way permissions interact with workers, and code that might be expecting to run in an environment without the `Deno` namespace actually seeing it, and then trying to do something, but not having the right permissions would break.
  - _Decision_ it is not burdensome to pass `deno: true` in the worker options, because `type: "module"` already has to be passed in Deno, and the risk of breaking changes for little to no value for the user isn't worth the risk, but we would like to correct the _mistake_ for Deno 2.0.
 - REPL `--eval` flag (#11317)
   - Python has this and it's nice
   - Really solves the problem of having a specific, easily repeatable, REPL context to work with
   - _Action_ progress forward, though specific semantics to debate.
author: kitsonk

title: Design Meeting 2021-08-12
body:
- Testing Face-Off 🥊 
  - In one corner @dsherret with a declarative approach
    - Solves the filtering use case better
    - Main drawback, extra features mean more syntax
    - Declarative approach more similar to existing popular JavaScript testing frameworks
  - In the other corner @lucacasonato with an imperative approach
    - Functionality added with an argument passed to the testing function.
    - It is _just_ code.
    - Can't filter subtests, but this is how it works in Go and that seems fine
  - Both solutions are backwards compatible
  - 🗳️  Team attending the meeting divided
  - _Action_ wider polling of the core team before a final decision is made, but we need to make one.
- NodeJS compatibility, what is our high-level strategy, goals, next steps?
  - Are we ok with the likes of Skypack and esm.sh, or are we actually trying to have full API compatibility with Node? "Node compatibility" is a nebulous concept.
  - `std/node` lacks major things like `http`, a lot of tools and workloads can't run on Deno because of it.
  - Do we see Node and Deno co-existing, or do we want to think of Node as "legacy"?  (Note, there was no clear decision on this question, it was just a conversation)
  - @kitsonk full parity would take forever and be "useless".  We should focus on particular workflows/workloads, fill in the gaps, and figure out a well supported migration path.
  - Should we put effort into documenting how to write code for both platforms? _Yes_
  - What Node has well established and Deno is generally lacking are well supported and performant DB drivers.  This is a problem, and problem for bring workloads over from Node to Deno.
  - Discussion again that we need to prioritise this space, if we try to do everything we will do nothing.
  - If we could say "you can run your Express server under Deno faster than Node" would that encourage adoption? _No clear answer_
  - @bartlomieju pointed out we had previously prioritised `std/node` here: https://github.com/denoland/deno_std/discussions/756
  - Further debate on if we focus on front-end workflows or backend servers.  There were a lot of good points.
  - _Action_ lack of `std/node/http` is a problem, no matter what we should solve that.  Skypack has said they would move to `std/node` if we had `http` which would also be a win.
  - _Action_ identify workflows/workloads we want to focus on and prioritise them, then figure out next steps.
- `Deno.ConnectTlsOptions#certFile` is a bad name (#11608)

title: Design Meeting 2021-08-19
body:
- Status of testing API proposals
  - The core team "voted" and the declarative approach had more support
  - That being said, @lucacasonato and @dsherret have being discussing together and with others outside the core team and feel that we will have some solid actions soon.
- Deno Configuration File
  - Reviewed the goals and non-goals (https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/3179#issuecomment-897393866)
  - Reviewed the "MVP" (https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/11686)
  - Discussed format, and how @ry @lucacasonato and @bartlomieju had explored other formats together and that only viable format is JSONC. We acknowledged that while we will continue to parse files with the `.json` extension as JSONC, we want to encourage people to use the `.jsonc` extension.
  - There was discussion lots of discussion about automatic lookup resolution logic, from what files names in what order and the "location" of the configuration file.  After a lot of discussion and various viewpoints, we acknowledged that while it would be great to have automatic discovery as part of the MVP, we should get out an MVP without it to get feedback from the community and then quickly determine the discovery logic.
- Can we share `op_read`/`op_write` between CLI and Deploy?
  - There are effectively 12 different resources that all have the same interface.
  - There was a debate on if this is over indexing on DRY versus just being the "convergent evolution".
  - There was no clear consensus on if this would really help anything and the change would be non-trivial.
- Plugin & FFI Discussion
  - Talked about feedback to date from the community
  - We acknowledged FFI is very limited.
  - We discussed how while it might feel seductive, Plugins are untenable.  They require exposing the innards of Deno and it is hard enough trying to keep the user space non-breaking changes and plugins add a whole new layer of compatibility issues, and people couple to even more "private" things, even if you say "please don't do this".
  - The preferred pattern we want to promote is making it easy to consume some of the "innards" of Deno via web assembly, versus enabling exposing internal APIs.  The biggest advantage is that people can still run "old" code while taking advantage of an updated runtime.  We have seen good proof points of this via things like SQLite running under Deno and crates like `deno_graph`.
  - We will continue to take feedback on FFI and what challenges and limitations the community are facing.

title: Design Meeting 2021-08-26
body:
- Discussion on micro task queue issues deferred, will be breakout meeting (#11731)
- `deno_lint` using the language server (denoland/deno_lint#805)
  - Using the language server to weed out "false positives" of linting diagnostics that would be otherwise returned, but type information would be required (e.g. fall-throughs that are fall-throughs because a function that has return type `never` is called)
  - Discussion around how `deno_lint` is _fast_ and spinning up of the tsc isolate is _slow_.  Having really fast rules and then every once in a while hitting a 1s delay when linting might be jarring from a UX perspective.
  - Discussion around how a swc type checker (or at least a partial one which could infer some types) would be more ideal way.
  - Discussion around how it would take a lot of re-architecting of CLI to be able to make it available
  - Not a small amount of work for limited upside, though valuable upside, so low priority.
  - _Action_ a low priority investigation/design
- Restructuring "tooling" code for re-usability
  - @bartlomieju brought up that there is always code that needs to be shared amongst the tools and that we have done some refactoring in CLI to co-locate that code, but then we also have seperate repos for `deno_graph`, `deno_lint`, `deno_doc`, etc.
  - @bartlomieju and @lucacasonato identified that some of the scope analysis logic in `deno_lint` might need to be shared with `deno_doc`
  - Is there a better way to share code like this?  A single "tooling" repo? Do we proactively refactor?
  - Updating swc is a pain point.  There is also a lot of "shared" code when it comes to managing the AST, do we need a `deno_ast` crate?
  - Discussion around multi-crate repos versus single crate repos.
  - Discussion around more release automation to take some of the pain points away.
  - _Action_ to not take any proactive steps, but keep discussing the _right_ choices as code needs to be shared/refactored.
- Supporting config for `deno fmt` (#3695 #11553)
  - @bartlomieju suggests at a minimum we need deal with file includes and excludes and tabs v. spaces
  - @lucacasonato strongly feels that no config is better, and that if spaces v tabs is an accessibility issue we should switch the code base to tabs.
  - Discussion around how Go gets away without a configurable formatter, but counter points that rustfmt allows a configuration.
  - Discussion around how Prettier has _minimal_ options and Prettier has become the _gold standard_ in JavaScript/TypeScript and how if we drew the line at supporting Prettier options, we could go tell people to have _arguments_ with Prettier about configurable options.
  - Discussion how a lack of a configuration is impeding adoption. Lots of "could possibly" with little specific examples of where a lack of a configuration was a barrier to adopting Deno (versus adopting just `deno fmt`)
  - Discussion around how the community likely wouldn't say "no please don't add configuration", so community support is a bit hard to base a decision off of.
  - Discussion around how tabs v spaces is a real issue, versus just a subjective one, while single-quotes v double-quotes and ASI are more "emotional" arguments, but real in some cases.
  - @lucacasonato actually gave a counter example to the argument, saying that contributing to a repo recently that was all single quote, he couldn't use save on format, trying to point out it would be great if everyone used the same style.  On the other hand, if you could configure it, you could use save on format and still contribute to a code base.
  - _Action_ @bartlomieju to put forward a proposal and to continue the discussion with the core team and the wider community. (#11857)
- Default Location/Default Origin/Local File Fetch proposal
  - There are two big "usability" issues with CLI that related to `--location` and `window.location`.
    - You cannot access `localStorage` without a `--location` flag, making it difficult to persist data, and with the desire to have `CacheStorage` and `IndexedDB` in the future, not having a solution means even more of a challenge.
    - You cannot currently fetch local files, but if you could, and you passed a relative path, what would happen? The standard says that you should use `window.location` as the base.
  - There is an internal design document about how to achieve have an internal origin that is derived from the environment to persistence without a `--location`.
  - Discussion how local file fetches, an implied `window.location` and an implied origin for persistence are 3 seperate topics.
  - _Action_ @kitsonk to break out the 3 problem spaces
  - _Action_ @kitsonk to raise the proposal for implied origin for public discussion (#11882)
  - _Action_ @kitsonk to pull together some thoughts on semantics for local file fetch and circulate among the core team for discussion at the next design meeting

title: Design Meeting 2021-09-09
body:
## Deno 2.0 Scope Discussion

We dedicated this meeting to discussing tentative Deno 2.0 discussion.  Based on the discussion we feel we are still looking at doing a 2.0 release in November.  Prior to the meeting we had collected candidate items, and the process we followed in the meeting:

- "Owner" briefly introduced the candidate item so that everyone had a shared understanding.
- We added any last minute entries.
- We voted against the items to prioritise the order of discussion.
- We mapped each item in order of priority against low and high value and desirability versus low and high effort, planning to focus on those things that had high value/desirability and low effort.

Based on that, we have the following scope items we are considering for Deno 2.0 at this point.  Note this is a working list, it is subject to change as some of the features get refined, scoped and investigated:

- Move JavaScript only "stuff" out of the Deno Namespace (#9795)
- Enable `Deno` namespace by default in workers (#8174)
- Don't type check be default (#11340)
- New subprocess API  (#11016, #5501, #11618)
- Turn TypeScript `useUnknownInCatchVariables` on (#11826)
- Remove deprecated `Deno.customInspect` (#10929)
- Lockfile generated by default (#11971)
- Switch JSX/TSX default constructors (#11186)
- Have a single configuration for TypeScript (#7732)
- Internal Origin for Persistance (#11882)
- Don't report check diagnostics for _external_ scripts by default (#11970)
- Use `--allow-import` for dynamic imports and workers (#8266)

There were a handful of issues we didn't have time to triage and will discuss them quickly at the start of next week's meeting:

- Make documentation test executable (#11782)
- Allow commas in args on the CLI (#6553, #9535)
- `NotCapable` error to distinguish between permissions and capabilities (#7394)
- Flatten `Deno.errors` into `Deno` namespace (#9646)
- Remove `Deno.read()` and `Deno.write()`

title: How to enable TypeScript `dom` lib via triple slash directives in `.js` files
body: I have a significant amount of isomorphic `.js` files that I intend to publish in a library that have have type checking enabled via a `// @ts-check` comment and JSDoc types throughout the code. This code uses the DOM (in React component hooks and event handlers, so it's ok during Deno SSR). Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be a way to enable the built-in TypeScript `dom` lib for types within `.js` files, using the triple slash directive `/// `: The Deno lint error being: ``` This triple-slash reference directive is not allowed in JavaScript In JavaScript only the `types` directive is allowed, like `/// ` ``` Why does this limitation exist? Can it be lifted? Using [a `lib` property in a `tsconfig.json` file](https://deno.land/manual@v1.13.2/typescript/configuration#targeting-deno-and-the-browser) is not a good solution, as only some files in the project are isomorphic, and these files will be published and deep imported by users so all types information needs to be contained within the file. I considered `/// ` and using a URL to a third-party Deno-compatible DOM `.d.ts` file, but this sucks because Deno ships with official DOM types so surely there is a way to reference them. It would be bad for my DOM types to conflict in user's projects that use the proper built-in DOM lib. Sometimes it feels like I'm the only one trying to use Deno to write isomorphic, published JS (see also https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/11362#issuecomment-909748559). I'm getting tired and desperate trying to solve this, so any help is greatly appreciated.

title: Design Meeting 2021-09-16
body:
- Deno 2.0 scheduled for release November 22nd
  - Agreement there is sufficient scope for a 2.0 release
  - Noted that TypeScript 4.5 should be GA'ed on the 16th
  - @ry raised a concern about how close that is to the release, but discussed that the beta and RC come well in advance to have a high confidence in the release.
- Discussion of additional scope items for 2.0.
  - We went through the list of un-triaged items as well as a few more "late additions".  The results are the following items were added to the scope:
    - `NotCapable` error to distinguish between permissions and capabilities (#7394)
    - Remove `Deno.read()` and `Deno.write()` (#12107)
    - JSON Modules (#7623) (TypeScript 4.5 should be the last piece of the puzzle for import assertions, so...)
    - op metrics refactoring/cleanup (#12109)
  - _Action_ @kitsonk to help ensure that all items have issues and are assigned to an "owner"
  - _Action_ all "owners" will be ready next week to discuss if their items are viable for Nov 22nd and if there are any risks or issues that might block it.
- Expanding the ecosystem
  - There was a long discussion on how we can help expand the ecosystem of Deno.  The perceived challenges:
    - Growth of users is relatively flat
    - It is speculated a lot of users shy away because adopting Deno seems hard or is hard
    - Perception that consuming Node.js code is hard (we don't believe it is, but the perception exists)
    - Using Deno as your development platform and sharing code with Node.js is hard (we feel this is a real problem)
  - @ry proposed a few actions to drive adoption of Deno and expand the ecosystem:
    - Allow extensionless imports under a _legacy_ flag.
    - Support bare specifiers for Node.js built-in modules.
  - @kitsonk proposed a counter proposal of:
    - Provide supported tooling to migrate a `package.json` to an import map and potentially other features to "convert" to a Deno-first project.
    - Add `deno emit` subcommand to emit a program as a set of ESM and/or CommonJS modules and a package.json for publishing to npm or other downstream consumption.
    - Complete `std` `node/*` modules
    - Consider a ruggadised polyfill for the `Deno` namespace to use with `deno emit`
  - There was a lot of discussion and debate around the extensionless imports which sort of came down to the following:
    - For: a belief that extensionless imports would allow a lot of existing TypeScript code to run under Deno and once there is a big enough headwind, they can be removed.
    - Against: a belief that extensionless imports doesn't actually solve compatibility problems, confuses users, likely will lead to huge support challenges and introduces _legacy_ features that will exist for ever.
    - Further actions were that we needed to do analysis and discussion on this topic.
  - The biggest concern around @kitsonk proposal was the concern that people would be resistant to rewriting all their code to use extensions, even if that were automated.

title: Shedding some light on the ecosystem
body:
There was some talk elsewhere on the less than desired rate of adoption Deno is getting. Just some thought on how to improve or work around what I think is the biggest barrier users have to actually start making stuff with deno - the small, relatively immature the ecosystem around it.

My personal experience with the core deno system has been wonderful. Simple, unopinionated, ergonomic, easy, highly browser compatible, modern, fast, stable-ish, consistently asynchronous, "fun", "clean", what's not to love? I feel like deno is on a point where the developer experience by itself is a great incentive for adoption. Judging from that, developers should be flocking around deno.

The main hurdle is the small amount and immaturity of third party modules. Obviously that situation can only be improved by deno gaining momentum/adoption. What we can do, though, is _helping users to find what good there already exist on the ecosystem._ 

The deno.land/x is a frustrating experience as there so much noise from unmaintained or just plain placeholder modules (early name-grabs and such). The star system does not really tell much whether the module is actually usable, mature or maintained. It's incredibly frustrating, hard detective work to find anything useful from there.

_Users need help finding modules they can actually use to accomplish stuff._  Rather than finding stuff from random articles around the net, I think it would be super helpful if there was some curated information on the official website. I propose two things:

1) 

A manually curated list of the "good stuff" somewhere clearly visibile on deno.land. To be on this list, for ease of maintenance and minimizing noise, the modules should:

- be somewhat stable/mature
- have a big enough scope (no one-liners or other tiny utility classes, but actual libraries)
- have a somewhat wide appeal for developers

Unfortunately at the current state of the ecosystem, this would not be a huge list, and it would be feasible to maintain manually. 

I understand if deno does not want to officially enforce some third party packages over others, but at this point I think users gravely need help navigating the ecosystem, and this would be a justified. 

Just a few examples of the modules that should be covered: oak, sqlite, canvas 

2) 

Another page again on deno.land, dedicated for users coming from node/NPM. This would involve identifying and listing the most popular, essential Node modules from NPM. For these, we would have notes on how to accomplish the same task in Deno. If any of the following things apply, it would be explained:

- is there a deno port
- can any of the newer web standard API's supported by deno be used to accomplish the same task (sqlite->webstorage)
- is there a deno package that answers the same problem (express->oak)
- can the NPM module in question be used "as is" in deno through esm.sh or such service, if so, how.


---------------
Just some thoughts for your consideration, I truly hope deno soon gains the momentum it deserves!
author: jtoppine

title: Major releases and breaking changes
body:
I was always under the impression that Deno would be backwards-compatible eternally, based on

> As of Deno 1.0.0, the Deno namespace APIs are stable. That means we will strive to make code working under 1.0.0 continue to work in future versions. - [Deno Manual, Stability](https://deno.land/manual@v1.14.1/runtime/stability) / [Release Schedule](https://deno.land/manual@v1.14.1/contributing/release_schedule)

But this is obviously not the case, as there are several breaking changes listed above. Could you release some information on how often major breaking version changes are expected in Deno? This seems like a fairly important question to consider, especially in enterprise context. For example, its strong backwards compatibility is arguably one of the core reasons Java has succeeded in staying relevant over the years. Personally I'm a big fan of Deno but would not really consider it in any large-scale project things keep changing so much.

In other words, don't you think it would be enough (at least regarding Deno namespace changes) to deprecate things, but not break them?

It's already happening, unfortunately, as a *lot* of Deno code found on the internet does in fact not work anymore (pre 1.0, especially). Often, imports in code samples are dead (removed from std, which itself is also still not stable). A phenomenon quite familiar from web browsing, but in programming languages, a rather unique aspect of Deno.

Anyway, what's the philosophy like for future breaking changes, especially long-term? I was unable to find any information on this

(Not taking into account TS version bumps)

(migrated from #12110, where you can also find answers on this by [@vwkd](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12110#issuecomment-927134246) and [@GJZwiers](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12110#issuecomment-927179184)

title: Best practice for including non-Deno TypeScript libraries
body:
What's the smoothest workflow for including/vendoring non-Deno TypeScript libraries *that aren't tightly coupled to Node* (e.g. [jsonc-parser](https://www.npmjs.com/package/jsonc-parser))?

Given these libraries aren't tightly coupled to Node, I thought this would be easy, but after reading and re-reading several sections of the Deno manual and searching the web, I'm still not seeing a great solution. Hopefully I just missed something obvious :)

The biggest issues I'm encountering are:

* Non-Deno TypeScript wants imports to not have ".ts" extension (whereas Deno requires an extension)
  * Obviously, this prevents everything from "just working"
* Finding/creating declaration (".d.ts") files is surprisingly difficult

# Approaches I've considered
## 1. See if someone already ported the library to Deno and published it to deno.land/x
I don't like this solution because it inserts a random, untrusted contributor into the workflow. Note: for the Microsoft library example above, I'm fine with assuming Microsoft isn't doing anything nefarious, so I may not even look at all the code before using the module in my project.

## 2. Fork the library and add ".ts" to all imports
This works, and the only new contributor is myself, but it is tedious and feels like something I shouldn't have to do. It also means I have to potentially redo some or all of this tedious work when I want to upgrade the module (especially if the module has been refactored).

This could be automated, but a robust solution would probably have to use the TypeScript compiler API, which I hoped I'd never have to deal with.

Edit: one more annoyance with this approach: if the library I'm importing has 100 source files, now I have 100 imports. If someone's aware of a TypeScript bundler that works, that would be a huge help here.

## 3. Use a Node-to-Deno CDN
In practice, this hasn't worked well for me. The biggest issue is that the type declarations are often missing or incorrect. I'm also a bit paranoid about trusting these CDNs, especially when they send me unreadable, minified JavaScript.

I'm not sure if the "missing declarations" problem is because NPM packages usually don't include declaration files in their "main" package (and instead toss the types into a separate `@types/` package, for good reason). Unhelpfully, I can't get "deno info" to tell me if types were provided at all (and I can't find any ".d.ts" files in my Deno cache).

## 4. Use WebPack/Rollup/esbuild
I don't have a lot of experience with these tools, but in every case, it looked like TypeScript *declaration file* support was bolted on with some random plugin that hasn't been updated in years.

As a particularly egregious example, WebPack's ts-loader plugin says to use [declaration-bundler-webpack-plugin](https://www.npmjs.com/package/declaration-bundler-webpack-plugin) for delcarations *which doesn't even provide a source code link on NPM*.

Edit: maybe there's a Deno-focused/compatible bundler I missed?

## 5. Create an import map to add ".ts" extensions
This works, but import maps are an application-level concept, so I can't really use them for a library I plan to publish. At least this seems trivial to automate.

## 6. Just run `tsc` and copy all the ".js" and ".d.ts" files it produces
This probably works... as long as the tsconfig.json produces output compatible with Deno. I'm hoping there's a better solution lurking somewhere.

Edit: this "works", but the declaration files still don't use ".ts" extensions in their imports...

## 7. Use `deno bundle` with an import map
Unfortunately, `deno bundle` [can't produce declaration files](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/3385)! Otherwise, this would probably be the easiest option to automate.

## 8. Copy the published lib and its corresponding types package from NPM
I'm hoping to remove NPM from my workflow, but this has worked for me in the recent past.

Edit: if the declarations are split across multiple files, I believe this will suffer from the same "no extensions" problem as option 6.

title: Best practice for publishing libraries that consume the Deno standard library
body:
I want to publish a "library" module (i.e. one that is intended to be consumed by other modules), and my module depends on functionality in Deno's standard library (deno.land/std).

**What's the best way to consume deno.land/std *in a library*?**

(I didn't see any information about this scenario in [Linking to external code](https://deno.land/manual@v1.16.4/linking_to_external_code#linking-to-third-party-code))

Considerations:

* I'd like the library to work on as many Deno versions as possible
* I don't want to have to update the module for each new Deno/std release (because there are *a lot* of releases)
* Let's *ignore unstable APIs* for now (because they generally require explicit versioning)

Edit to add: this situation for Deno's standard library is unique in that the std version is updated often, all the modules are lumped into a single library (with one version), and the std versions are mapped to specific Deno versions (I assume mainly for unstable APIs... hopefully not much else!).

The two options I see are:

1. Import without a version (`https://deno.land/std/testing/asserts.ts`)
2. Import with a version (`https://deno.land/std@0.117.0/testing/asserts.ts`)

The first option is attractive, but it seems fragile (especially when Deno 2.0 arrives). The second option is probably best, but I don't like that it duplicates code unless consumers use an import map to align std versions.

Some notes follow:

# Import without a version
Note: I haven't found a module that does this.

I see a number of benefits to this:

* My library doesn't need to be updated as bugs are fixed in the standard library
* Multiple libraries will end up using the same standard library code (instead of whatever version the library author happened to use)

But there are significant drawbacks:

* **What happens when Deno hits 2.0?** Does my module break? Or is `std` renamed to `std2`? :)
* My library could break if the standard library subtly changes some behavior I depended upon (intentionally or unintentionally)

# Import with a version
Benefits:

* I know exactly what code is running (... until someone uses an import map)
* No worries about Deno 2.0 :)

Downsides:

* If there's a bug in the version of the standard library I use, either I'll have to update the module or all consumers will have to use an import map (and of course an import map can introduce bugs if there are subtle behavior changes between std versions)
* When consuming N different libraries, I'll be pulling in potentially N different copies of standard library modules (unless I use an import map)

Still, this seems like the most reliable option. Consumers that want to align std versions need to use an import map (and hope nothing breaks!), e.g. the following maps `@0.117.0` and `@0.116.0` to `@0.113.0` (I just made up the version numbers):

```json
{
    "imports": {
        "https://deno.land/std@0.117.0/": "https://deno.land/std@0.113.0/",
        "https://deno.land/std@0.116.0/": "https://deno.land/std@0.113.0/"
    }
}
```

title: Add support of ping/pong frames to WebSocket class
body:
Since the version 0.118.0 of `deno_std`, `ws` module was removed. The documentation says to use [`Deno.upgradeWebSocket()`](https://doc.deno.land/deno/stable/~/Deno.upgradeWebSocket) API instead. This function returns `{ response: Response, socket: WebSocket }` where [`WebSocket`](https://doc.deno.land/deno/stable/~/WebSocket) is a type that, as I understand, the authors of Deno aim to use both for client-side and server-side WebSockets. 

The `WebSocket` class in Deno has been implemented in accordance with W3C WebSocket API, which is the standard meant primarily for browsers. It is unfortunate that the control over ping/pong frames [is not exposed](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/web-sockets.html#ping-and-pong-frames) through this API. Browsers do not provide to the scripts they run any means to deliberately send ping frames to the server, or to detect incoming pings. Thankfully, browsers, as well as all conforming implementations at least [automatically respond](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455#section-5.5.2) to pings when the other party sends them.

It is then crucial that the other party—server—has control over ping/pong frames. This control is necessary for latency instrumentation, maintaining of NAT mappings and timely detection of broken connections ([example from ws, a node.js library](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ws#how-to-detect-and-close-broken-connections)). Contrary to what some may believe, TCP just by itself does not provide these features. Broken TCP connections [can be present for a very long time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCP_half-open#:~:text=According%20to%20RFC%20793%2C%20a,for%20unbounded%20periods%20of%20time.) without any notification to the other party!

My question is whether the authors of Deno consider it feasible to add methods to send ping/pong frames and events to act upon their receipt to the `WebSocket` class.

title: best practice for private local common modules?
body:
## Use Case

a **local private** common utils module that used by multiple independent other projects.
Currently, I think of two ways: 1. import localhost URL. 2. import files

## import localhost URL
1. start a local file-server at common-module's parent directory
2. `import {...} from "http://localhost:port/a-common-module/mod.ts"`
3. `deno run -r main.ts`

Note:
1. In this way, different projects use the **same** import URL.
2. Because deno run will cache remote(including localhost) modules, to keep the common module update, you needs to use the --reload(-r) option to run in other projects.

## import file directly
For example, `import {...} from "../../some-path/all-local-modules/a-module"`.

But local projects in different locations need to use **different** relative import path.

## Question
Is this the best practice for private local common modules?

title: deno vendor should check compressed archive into git by default
body:
so I have been mulling over the new `deno vendor` command. It seems like a very useful tool for safety, and robustness. However, I suspect I will find two things about it annoying:
1. editor fuzzy file searches will include the `./vendor` folder by default
2. updating dependencies will explode git history

1 is solveable locally, but becomes annoying for contributors. The best you can do is find something common editors read from like an `.editorconfig` and add notes to the readme.
2 is another issue, which will make PRs harder to sift through and increase the size of repo significantly over time.

So, I had a thought, what if `deno vendor` did two things. The first is download all files into a `./vendor` folder like it already does, but the second is to create an archive `./vendor.tar.gz` (or `./vendor.zip`) which is simply the vendor file compressed. The idea is, that the uncompressed vendor folder will be gitignored and `vendor.tar.gz` will be checked into git. Updating deps should change both the uncompressed vendor folder and the compressed vendor.tar.gz file. Git changes to those dependencies will still be reflected in version numbers where deps are used, so its not like we need the code diffs on deps.


This is something that can be built outside of deno now pretty simply, just with a script like so:
```bash
#! /bin/bash

tar xzvf ./vendor.tar.gz
```

the value in including this workflow in deno though, would be that deno could include some magic in `deno run` that detects if the uncompressed vendor folder and the compressed vendor.tar.gz file have become out of sync (like when a `git pull` is done), and then uncompress vendor.tar.gz before executing the program.

title: How to Deno.listen on existing file descriptor?
body:
Hello,

I apologize if this has already been answered, I looked everywhere I could - I promise!

How does one use Deno.listen() to listen on an existing file descriptor / resource?
**OR**
Please allow Deno.listen() to listen on existing file descriptors / resources.

Similarly Deno.read(), Deno.write(), etc. allows one to read/write/etc. from a given resource id (which is obviously an essential function as files are a widely adopted system concept). Using the Deno documentation I was able to successfully utilize Deno.listen() to simultaneously create a socket() resource and to bind() to it, which is neat, but in some particular instances one would prefer not to (or can not) do that first step as there already exists a socket (that can still be bound to). 

For example, the popular software [spawn-fcgi](https://linux.die.net/man/1/spawn-fcgi) creates a socket, executes a specified process, and assigns the socket to fd 0. Systemd is also a now popular software that creates a socket for your process (but I think it assigns it to fd 3?).

If this feature isn't yet available, may I suggest this syntax: `Deno.listen(0)` where 0 represents Deno's first resource. This makes it similar to Deno's read(), write(), etc functions and also virtually every other popular definition of listen() (see both [posix](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/listen.html) and win32). I'd greatly prefer that syntax, but if that isn't acceptable then the next obvious form would be `Deno.listen({rid: 0})`. Additionally, in my opinion `Deno.listen({transport: "rid", rid: 0})` or similar is **not** preferable, but I also realize that it may be required if Deno needs to know whether the socket is a datagram socket or not.

Also if this feature isn't yet available, could someone direct me towards some literature that illustrates how to utilize either op calls or Deno's newer FFI API to just use the system's listen() functionality in an async manner? With the instance I have in mind FFI and "unstable" is fine and listen() is available, but Deno.run() is not (nor is any foreign subprocessing functions). 

Thank you!

Update: I just discovered [op_net_accept](https://github.com/denoland/deno/blob/main/ext/net/ops.rs#L162) which I'll attempt to experiment with, but some usage hints would still be appreciated.

title: `deno task` feedback
body:
I've been using `deno task` for a bit now and [the blog post](https://deno.com/blog/v1.20#:~:text=We%20would%20appreciate%20your%20feedback%20to%20help%20shape%20this%20feature.) was asking for feedback. I'm running into some minor usability issues so I figured I'd post them here.

### Introduction

First let me describe how I was running scripts before `deno task` was added. Basically all scripts have a shebang at the top of the file similar to what many of the scripts in the Deno project use:

https://github.com/denoland/deno/blob/e55dee7fd894f705a0268a4734b00197021f0617/tools/format.js#L1-L2

I like this method because it keeps the required permissions close to the actual file, and running the script is extremely simple because all you have to do is run `./tools/format.js`.

But the downside is... it doesn't work very well on Windows. Maybe I'm missing a simple solution for this, but as far as I can tell `/usr/bin/env` is not really a thing on Windows, and shebang support isn't great either. So Windows users are stuck with having to run scripts using `deno run` while trying to figure out what the required permissions are (or running with `-A`).
This wasn't a huge problem for me though. I'm mostly developing on macOS, so I was using shebangs for now, though I did want to have better cross platform support eventually. 

### `deno task` to the rescue

`deno task` makes it possible to easily run scripts cross platform, but the benefits from the shebang method are now gone:

- Permissions are no longer in the same file as the main entry point.
- `deno task build -- --dev` is more cumbersome to write than `./build.js --dev`
- I reckon this issue is a bit more niche, but I feel the need to mention it anyway: Autocomplete for files no longer works when using `deno task`. I guess this depends on your shell as well, but before I used to do `./test.js path/to/file.test.js`, where the last part of the command would get autocompleted by my shell. This is not the case with `deno task test -- path/to/file.test.js`. I suppose this is also caused by `deno completions` being installed.

### Potential solutions

I'm currently using both methods, so every script has both a task configured as well as a shebang. That way Windows users can use `deno task build` and unix users can keep using `./build.js`. But now there's two places where arguments need to be updated. If a developer on a unix system makes a change that requires different permissions they might only update the shebang, causing the `deno task` to break. And vice versa for developers using Windows.

Perhaps something like https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12763 would make this easier. Though this won't take care of other arguments such as `--unstable`. And the location of the permissions would still be separate from the main entry point.

Though I think what I would prefer the most is if `deno task` were able to parse `/usr/bin/env` shebangs somehow. This way the file itself could use a `#!/usr/bin/env` shebang, and the configured task would only need to point to the file. Maybe a task could even look like

```
"tasks": {
    "build": "./build.js"
}
```

This already works on unix, on Windows it gives an error. This way, unix users could keep running files like `./build.js`, and systems that don't support running files like this could use the tasks.
I'm not sure how far you'd want to go with making the tasks run cross platform. Since not only would this have to be able to handle running files via `./` syntax, it would also have to parse shebangs and implement `/usr/bin/env` somehow. Sounds like this is very much out of scope for Deno, but it would solve all issues mentioned above.

### Conclusion

Anyway, those are my ramblings. Not sure how big of an issue this really is. I could certainly live with the current situation, I just feel like DX could be better here. Maybe someone knows a neat trick that allows you to run files on Windows in a similar manner. That would eliminate the need for tasks like these altogether.

title: Automatic Body Compression Clarification
body:
It should be made clear in the manual how Deno internally handles automatic body compression:

1. Does Deno internally maintain a cache of compressed bodies?
2. If so, how long do those cache entries last?

If Deno does not maintain a cache, it could be inefficient for servers with high traffic to compress bodies upon every request, especially during a denial-of-service attack.

If Deno does maintain a cache, it is not specified how long cache entries last, and long-lived servers may end up keeping cache entries that are no longer needed.

A potential solution would be to specify that Deno does indeed utilize a cache, and to provide a Deno API to inspect/remove entries from such a cache.

title: Default Deno.bench warmups may not be high enough for some CI runners
body:
Recently I have been benchmarking with `Deno.bench` and having fun, although it seems that on some CI runners the default 1000 warmups is not sufficient. On the Ubuntu runner in Github Actions in particular there is a major difference in the measured time of whatever benchmark is run first, compared to other runners and my local machine.

For example, I am benching a JS and WASM implementation of a string distance algorithm. The results are very consistent on my local setup and the MacOS/Windows runners: JS is faster on relatively short strings while WASM is faster on long ones:

```
bench Myers 32bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 1,035 ns/iter (700..59,100 ns/iter) ok (17ms)
bench Myers 32bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 2,726 ns/iter (2,400..8,900 ns/iter) ok (12ms)
bench Myers 1024bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 425,071 ns/iter (401,300..565,900 ns/iter) ok (884ms)
bench Myers 1024bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 80,577 ns/iter (78,500..122,900 ns/iter) ok (166ms)
```

On the Ubuntu runner though, there is a time anomaly in the first bench, showing a much higher average `ns/iter`:

```
bench Myers 32bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 10,783 ns/iter (9,300..88,499 ns/iter) ok (35ms)
bench Myers 32bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 6,350 ns/iter (3,400..60,500 ns/iter) ok (24ms)
bench Myers 1024bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 673,224 ns/iter (556,596..3,331,975 ns/iter) ok (1s)
bench Myers 1024bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 152,748 ns/iter (118,299..4,364,268 ns/iter) ok (294ms)
```

I can actually shift the extra time in the CI to a different benchmark by having it run first:

```
bench test bench JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 9,218 ns/iter (1,400..96,701 ns/iter) ok (59ms)
bench Myers 32bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 1,322 ns/iter (1,000..5,600 ns/iter) ok (16ms)
bench Myers 32bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 4,417 ns/iter (4,300..22,500 ns/iter) ok (33ms)
bench Myers 1024bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 750,559 ns/iter (736,909..3,943,152 ns/iter) ok (1s)
bench Myers 1024bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 141,181 ns/iter (140,301..225,303 ns/iter) ok (290ms)
```

Using more warmups solves this problem, somewhere around 3000-5000 giving results that are more in line with my expectation:

```
bench Myers 32bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 1,470 ns/iter (1,100..64,300 ns/iter) ok (47ms)
bench Myers 32bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 4,473 ns/iter (4,100..129,601 ns/iter) ok (17ms)
bench Myers 1024bp string JavaScript ... 1000 iterations 739,221 ns/iter (731,106..1,865,416 ns/iter) ok (1s)
bench Myers 1024bp string WebAssembly ... 1000 iterations 144,435 ns/iter (143,501..224,102 ns/iter) ok (298ms)
```

Don't know if anyone else has encountered something similar, but this made me wonder if the default warmups for `Deno.bench` should be higher, assuming more people will be using this in CI environments in the future.
author: GJZwiers

title: `deno test` printer feedback
body:
I've been using deno as a test runner for some time now, and after having written about 900 tests, I've found a few issues with the way test results are printed. I'm not sure about any future plans for this, and I didn't want to create a separate ticket for every issue I had. So I figured I'd post something here first.

## Finding the source of a failing test
When a test fails, the first thing you want to do is go to source code of the failing test in order to find out what exactly the test is about. Right now this is not very easy, you can do one of the following:
 - Look for a path in the stack trace of the failing test, but sometimes stack traces are long and you won't be able to find the file you need right away.
 - Scroll up to your test results and find the one that says 'FAILED' then look up a few lines until you see the path of the file.
 - Use your ide to search for the name of the test in all your files, and hope that another file with a similar test name doesn't exist.

### Possible solutions:

 - https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/13586 would certainlly help, but not eliminate the issue entirely
 - In the list of test results, print the `running n tests from file:///path/to/file.test.js` with a different color. That way when you scroll up you can immediately distinguish tests that come from one specific file.
 - Print the path of a failing test above the error. Currently the name of the test is already printed, but often this is not enough. Say you have a file `calculator.test.js` with test name `"it adds two numbers together"` and only the name is printed, it is not immediately clear that this test is from `calculator.test.js` rather than another file that might have a similar test.
 - Print the path above the final list of failures. This could look similar to how the first list of test results look, where it prints the path only once if multiple tests in a single file fail.

## It's hard to distinguish `console.log()` calls from test results
Right now if code calls `console.log` the result gets appended in between `[test name] ...` and `ok` without any new lines, and multiple calls print double new lines in between every call.
The same happens with `Check https://example.com/file.js` being printed when dynamically importing files.

For instance, this test, which dynamically imports blob urls:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2737650/160927670-d88a76d2-c298-4094-a301-80a5ac80a09c.png)

Though I reckon this would be pretty nontrivial, it seems logging code is already pretty scattered accross the codebase (see https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/13001).

## Hiding test results if they don't fail
If I remember correctly, the test runner used by [the Chrome DevTools team](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-frontend) simply shows a progress bar of all the tests and only failing tests are reported. I believe they use Mocha.

In a way I like it because it's a lot easier to find failing tests, since you don't have to scroll through all the test results. And if you have a huge amount of tests, where one of the first ones fails, you won't have to wait for the entire suite to finish because the error would get printed right away.

But on the other hand I kind of like the verbosity that Deno has right now. Seeing a whole bunch of green ok's is pretty satisfying.

## A quick mockup
Here's a quick mockup of what some of these changes could look like.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2737650/160925198-9b11111b-465b-4574-b4b4-ecf17d31bbd2.png)

<!--https://github.com/denoland/deno/files/8384024/testmockup.js.zip-->

I think it's a lot easier to visually parse like this. Not sure how feasible it would be to print error messages in red though. Since error messages might have custom color formatting. Maybe they should only be printed in red if the error message does not contain any ansi codes.

### Recap
Quick recap of all the changes:
- print file paths in the results with a different color
- add file paths to the errors section
- add file paths to the failures section
- print error messages with a red color
- divide the tests in three sections: "results", "errors" and "failures" and print each section in yellow
- Better printing of `console.log()` calls in between the results (not shown in the mockup)

Feel free to let me know if these changes are desirable (or if only a subset of them are), I'd be glad to create a new ticket for each of these.

title: Design for platform dependent operations
body:
Perspective:

I use Deno as a replacement for bash/powershell (which has been fantastic BTW). I've run into a handful of limitations like checking if a command is valid (if it's in the path), or getting the owner of a file (as a username not UID), etc.

Cases being considered :

- macOS file attributes
- selinux permission system
- redox OS
- all the non-POSIX garbage in Windows


Discussion:

There are currently a few parts of the Deno API that behave differently depending on the OS. And I think there's quite a few more in unstable that are also not universal.

I'd like to propose having a separate part of the API for OS-specific functions, while keeping the core Deno API a bit more pure in terms of cross-platform-ness. For example, instead of having chmod-permissions married to Deno, it could be under `Deno.os.unix.chmod`. And instead of highly specific vanilla-linux result for `lstat` the returned value could contain abstracted valuest that are likely to work cross platform.

1. I think this would help core devs, since cross platform API design is much much harder than OS specific API design. Platform specific can be done first giving users the functionality they need, then later a cross-platform API can be designed, tested, and implemented.
2. It prevents bloat to the core Deno API
3. It reduces the number of edgecases, we don't have to think "does Deno.symlink work for just Unix or also windows?" 
4. It would make it easy when reading a codebase to see OS specific methods at a glance.

title: Suggestion: Name the OS-interacting functions semantically, instead of after the POSIX syscall names
body:
I'm sure this breaks a *lot* of people's well-worn habits so apologies in advance - my intentions are pure! Don't hurt me! 

The suggestion: Deno & other interpreters should stop using the C syscall names verbatim for the interpreter's exposed API function names (see: [Deno.lstat](https://doc.deno.land/deno/stable/~/Deno.lstat)). 

**We should absolutely still clearly document the underlying system calls being made in each Deno API function**, to: 

- demystify what the interpreter's doing, and so 
- C/Unix veterans can quickly search up the right Deno function corresponding to the functionality they're used to, 

but the original names are *bad, bad, bad* names. They were chosen in an era with totally different considerations, where programs stored as text took up significant space, and weren't being compressed. Text editors didn't autocomplete, let alone suggest function names. The entire POSIX and C landscape is named this way and I'm sure most of us are even fond of the idiosyncratic names, but we need to acknowledge that almost all the names are **awful**. Even when they're a single valid word they're often not descriptive or intuitive (`fork`/`tee`), some are arbitrarily truncated (`exec`), they have no word delimiters so you sometimes need to guess the intended words (`flock`), some of them are like weird half-acronyms (`chown`), and in the context of JS / Deno, **they appear to the uninitiated as totally arbitrary exceptions to naming/style conventions** (which is bad no matter what you think of the inherent quality of the POSIX names). 

Another advantage of abstracting away from the POSIX names is that it makes development more cross-platform in a human/social sense - if a dev's targeting Windows they don't even need to know the Linux or Mac internal names for things to use Deno fully.

To get the ball rolling: `stat` / `lstat` / `fstat`  could be rolled into one function and exposed as something like:
```typescript 
fileInfo(file: string, followSymlinks: boolean = true)
``` 

This way, you have `fileInfo()` returning a [FileInfo](https://doc.deno.land/deno/stable/~/Deno.FileInfo) object - pretty straightfoward. We could even go implicit and name it `status()`, `attributes()` or `properties()`, given almost every FS path points to some kind of "file". I think the majority of people would immediately understand "status/attributes/properties" refers to the file the given path refers to, rather than the path string itself.

title: test tags
body:
I want a way to easily run a subset of tests based on tags (unit, integration, e2e, fast, slow, smoke, etc.).

## Status quo

[Command line filtering](https://deno.land/manual/testing#command-line-filtering) makes this possible with patterns but it is awkward:

**something.test.ts**
```ts
Deno.test("something tag::slow tag::integration", () => {/* ... */});
```

**example**
```sh
deno test --filter "/\btag::slow\b/" # "tag::slow" isn't sufficient as it would match "tag::slowest", etc.
```

Using negative lookaheads (which I'm not even sure `deno test --filter` supports) is even more awkward for specifying tags _not_ to run and patterns get more complex when you want to include some tags but not other.

Encoding tags into test names also creates noise in the test report that isn't desirable, especially when tests have multiple tags.

## Proposal

```ts
declare namespace Deno {
  interface TestDefinition {
    tags?: string[];
  }
}
```

**something.test.ts**
```ts
Deno.test("something", { tags: ["slow", "integration"] }, () => {/* ... */});
```

### Command line tag expression ideas

<details>
<summary>JavaScript-like boolean operators</summary>

```sh
deno test --tags slow
deno test --tags 'fast && smoke'
deno test --tags 'e2e && !slow'
deno test --tags '(fast || smoke) && !slow'
```

note that `!` has to be used inside single quotes (`'`) rather than double quotes (`"`)

</details>

<details>
<summary>predicate-like</summary>

```sh
deno test --tags "slow"
deno test --tags "fast and slow"
deno test --tags "e2e and not(slow)"
deno test --tags "(fast or smoke) and not(slow)"
```

note that `not()` is function-like, this might not be necessary but made sense at the time of writing

</details>

<details>
<summary>cucumber-like</summary>

```sh
deno test --tags "@slow"
deno test --tags "@fast and @slow"
deno test --tags "@e2e and not @slow"
deno test --tags "(@fast or @smoke) and not @slow"
```

see [Tag expressions - Cucumber Reference - Cucumber Documentation](https://cucumber.io/docs/cucumber/api/?lang=javascript#tag-expressions)

</details>

author: reggi

title: Ideas around import_map tooling.
body:
Forgive me if I'm naieve I'm not sure what already exists, please point me in the right direction if this is a non-issue or solved problem.

Because deno import maps [don't chain recursively](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/73429995/deno-local-import-map-not-working-recursively/73430479#73430479) you can't really use them in modules unless the project also implements the same imports. This can be a pain. 

I'd love some third-party scripts / tooling around this, and I'm sure others will as well here are some ideas perhaps projects will surface that already exist or this will guide people to what needs to be created.

It seems that `import_maps` serve two purposes, 

1) make it more convient for devs to use a remote module
2) be able to change the dep of a dep (something that's broken upstream)

I think most of this tooling focuses on (1), but if someone upstream fixes an issue upstream I want that to be fixed for me too see https://github.com/eveningkid/denodb/issues/348#issuecomment-1221372635.

## Deno adding multiple `import_maps` to `deno.json`? 

Some of these tools become irrelevant if Deno just handles this out of the box. As of right now you can only have one `import_map` but we could make it an array? An array that supports urls? 👀

## Potential Commands

### Merge `import_maps`

Abiding by the one `import_map` standard then I think the right way to do this is to have a `import_maps` directory and save a snapshot of the current custom imports. Then new import files are downloaded and put into this directory.  The tool then merges all the import maps and spits out a new single `./import_map.json`. Errors occur if there's conflicts. This will allow you to "undo" a merge because all the files are separate, all you have to do is remove the file.

`import_maps merge`

### Download single `import_map`

Check a url for ./import_map.json and pull into your project. The name of the source can be included via metadata file or in the json, and this allows the ability to revert / remove imports. The api could look like this:

`import_maps download http://deno.land/x/example@1.1.1`

### Download project-wide `import_maps`

Scan all the code in a deno project, check all potental deps for import maps, download them all.

`import_maps find ./main.ts`

### Replace map key with dep `import_maps`

This would go through the codebase and replace (inline) all the import maps with their value / url counterparts.

`import_maps replace-map-key-with-dep`

### Replace dep with map key `import_maps`

This would go through the codebase and replace (inline) all the urls with their import_map key counterparts.

`import_maps replace-dep-with-map-key`

## Show unused `import_maps`

This would give you a readout of any import maps that aren't being used.

## Remove unused `import_maps`

This would remove any unused import maps from `./import_maps.json`.

## Import map local-file generator

You could just use the import maps to generate local files, like this:

This:

`./import_maps.json`
```json
{
   "imports": {
        "lodash": "https://deno.land/x/lodash@4.17.19"
    }
}
```

Generates this: 

`./imports/lodash.ts`
```ts
export * from 'https://deno.land/x/lodash@4.17.19"
```

Usage like this:

`./main.ts`
```ts
export * from './imports/loadsh"
```

title: Guidelines on how to author code with less dependencies
body:
# Context

I've been messing around with creating a calendar scheduling app. I wanted a simple way someone could pass in time-slot availability, this is a bit annoying to do via just JSON with intervals and breaks in between and days of the week that sort of stuff. 

Something like [this](https://github.com/reggi/deno-monorepo/blob/main/calendar/time/week_test.ts):

```ts
Week
  .weekdays(Span.nineToFive.every(30).excludeSpan(Span.lunch))
   .weekend(Span.lunch.every(30))
```

# What's the best way to author a Deno module?

While I know there's many ways to do any given thing, It left me thinking **what's the best way to author a module** so that people  using it don't have to download all the files in the module. Let me give some examples:

1. If I wrote everything in one file you have to all the code, even unused code, but one request
2. If I wrote every function / class in separate files you'd have only code you need, but many requests

![Untitled-2022-08-24-1109](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/296798/186455571-2d07d240-3ae9-41f8-8645-e65309ff49c4.png)

So there's a spectrum and both ends are not great. I'm curious if there's a different way to look at this? Something I'm missing.

If people author code-in-classes (which I tried to stay away from in that example, you have to download the entire class, you can't really provide parts of a class. So functions-first is necessary. Classes in my example are just glue / wrappers around the functions (except when classes get passed around, which I'd have to undo, functions can't take classes as input).

## Options

1. A linter
2. Dynamic Files

### Linter

A linter that specializes in guiding authors to best practices when it comes to authoring code with less dependencies would be an amazing alternative. Advising people to not author hefty classes that all connect directly?

### Dynamic Files

This would mean the url builds a single file with all the code in it.

This is an idea adjacent to the post here about hosting your own [deno module server](https://github.com/denoland/deno/discussions/15550).  I'm dubbing this in the category of "#serverMagic" (id like a whole discussion on different "#serverMagic" techniques). 

This idea would be source-tree-shaking the modules served, with the URL you have the ability to target a specific export within a file via query parameter, or even path, all bets are off when your generating dynamic TS. 

I'm equally attracted to the idea of dynamically generated modules from the server and of the mind that you should just serve a single file no tricks.

I'm curious what other people's thoughts are.

my-native-folder/

title: New deno mirror on npmjs.org?
body:
Hi there, 

I would like to have an official deno binary mirror on npmjs.org.

## TL;DR Questions 

@ry @lucacasonato 

(Target for these questions is mostly the deno company) 

1. Do you want to build an official deno binary mirror package on npmjs.org? 

2. If not, would you allow me to start/do it? (See my use-case and my plan below)

3. Would you be down to let me contribute my solution to an official deno namespace on npmjs? (If you have any and clearly after review from the deno company) 

## Use-Case

I work at a company behind a firewall (as many people).

I would like to use deno as a lightweight scripting environment to avoid long-running npm installs in ci. 

I also would like to use deno'a fresh package for lightweight status pages about our running services. 

I'm able to install deno on my Developer machine, since it doesn't need admin rights. 
However, I can't install it in CI/CD environment, because the Jenkins server has no real internet connection. 

_A short description of our Jenkins environment: 
We have an openshift kubernetes cluster, which contains the Jenkins server. Each build node for this Jenkins is an ephemeral container which gets started for each individual build und then discarded.
Note: I can't add a new base image for build nodes, due to permissions._

The only solution we have to get dependencies on the Jenkins build nodes is a company-wide nexus npm proxy registry. 

## What I tried before 

I tried to install deno via official methods on the Jenkins build runners. This has several drawbacks: 

1. I have to provide the deno executable via my projects git repo, since I can't load it from the internet. 
(Which is a huuuuge pain in the ass already, due to binaries in the git repo) 

2. The installation does not persist due to these ephemeral build nodes. This increases complexity of build scripts (due to not having deno in the main PATH) and all 'global' scripts I would install with deno would have to be installed with every build run.

## My Proposed Solution
_This is the proposal for the question in TL;DR Section above, how I would do it!_

1. I would like to set up a git repo, which gets notified of each new deno binary release. 
Options: 
- maybe there is a webhook somewhere for that? 
- or I have to Setup a small deno.deploy service, which regularly checks the version of the deno executable at the normal download endpoint. 

After that: 
2. When a new deno binary is out, this event should trigger a GitHub actions pipeline, which downloads the new binaries and packages them into a node package. 

One open question for that is: How to structure the npm package best? 

- Can we add different os  binaries in the package.json bin fields for npm to pick the right one to execute based on host system? 

- Or do we have to write a little js loader in node to know which executable to run based on the host os? 

- could we execute this os-detection earlier (for example in the preinstall hook) to not having to launch deno through nodejs every time?

- if we cannot do that, do we release one deno package per system and arch and add that to the naming of the package?

3. Lastly these packages simply need to be published on npmjs.org

I'm very interested in the answers!

title: Top-level function arrow syntax
body:
I see in [Deno Style Guide](https://deno.land/manual@v1.25.4/contributing/style_guide) a section called [Top-level functions should not use arrow syntax.](https://deno.land/manual@v1.25.4/contributing/style_guide#top-level-functions-should-not-use-arrow-syntax) I understand that the guide "is not meant as a general style guide for users of Deno" but when trying to make decisions on my own style guides it is often helpful to understand the reasons behind other style guides.

Why does Deno runtime and standard library use the `function` keyword at the top-level instead of arrow functions?

e.g. Is the thinking that doing so clearly marks functions as functions (readability)? Is it so that hoisting can be leveraged (some folks find such a feature desirable while others do not)?

There are scope differences at runtime but something that I was surprised to learn this morning is that top-level functions are added to global scope which I'm not sure I like (see [this answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/38480257/3255152) to [What are the advantages/disadvantages for creating a top level function in ES6 with arrows or without?](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38479859/what-are-the-advantages-disadvantages-for-creating-a-top-level-function-in-es6-w)).

Personally I've historically preferred `function` as I find it reads better, it is consistent with generator syntax (no arrow option there), and I can prefix a named function with `export default` (can't be done with named arrow functions).

title: Add flag for filtering env-variables on Deno.env access
body:
While it is great that `--allow-env=*` raises an exception, when a program uses a not permitted env variable, I think in contrast to other `--allow-*` Permissions of `deno run` the pattern is not enough for env access.

In the wild many libraries want to access possibly more Env-Variables than a programm writer want to grant access to. Especiall when you see lib-authors see using `Deno.env.toObject()` or similar. This results oft in providing access to all the Environment via `--allow-env` possibly introducing more security vulnerabilities. 

I would love to see a `deno run` option like `--grant-env` (or something similar), that actually silently does not give access to a variable without failing. 

Especially with the `npm` world becoming more accessible, the deno permission spirit faces lots of libraries written in a different mindset, eagerly reading all env variables without hesitation. I think a solution as described would improve the security of deno apps a lot.

**As an example:**

```
export PORT=3001;
echo "console.log(Deno.env.get('PORT'))" | deno run --allow-env=PORT - # => 3001
echo "console.log(Deno.env.get('PORT'))" | deno run - # fails with 'PermissionDenied: Requires env access to "PORT"'

echo "console.log(Deno.env.get('PORT'))" | deno run --grant-env=DEBUG --allow-env - # => null
echo "console.log(Deno.env.get('PORT'))" | deno run --grant-env=PORT --allow-env -  # => 3001
```

So `--allow-env` would allow a user to ask for `PORT`, but when `--grant-env` is specified, but not defining `PORT`, it is silently empty and result in an empty string.

title: Deno types in `eslint`/`tsc` without VSCode extension?
body:
We have an existing Node.js development environment with many existing Node.js packages/apps in a monorepo. Everything in our repository is written in TypeScript, linted with `eslint`, and type checked with `tsc`.

We've recently added a Remix + Deno Deploy app to our repository. In our dev environment we use `remix watch` and `deno run`; to deploy the app we run `remix build` and deploy `build/index.js` to Deno Deploy.

This required a few workarounds, like patching the Remix `esbuild` config, and running `deno types > deno.d.ts` (and then removing `/// <reference no-default-lib="true" />`) to help ESLint and TypeScript understand things like `Deno.env`. But everything seems to be working; we're successfully developing a Deno app in a Node.js development environment, which is a great first step toward a larger adoption of Deno.

One part I'm not happy with, is that there doesn't seem to be a way to teach ESLint and TypeScript how to understand `deno.land` imports, so that our adoption of Deno can be gradual and seamless. `deno lint` is too limited, and we don't want two separate code quality solutions in one repository; we're also not interested in a VS Code extension, which also wrongly assumes our entire repository and development environment would adopt Deno in one big bang. What we're looking for are tools for gradual adoption in a large existing codebase, which is realistically the only way we'll adopt other parts of Deno besides Deno Deploy.

Are there solutions for any of this? Any guidance would be appreciated, thanks!
