author: ShooterIT

title: AOF annotations
body:
As we know, in AOF, there are only Redis commands,  in some cases, we may want to know context of commands for updating database. In RocksDB, it allows us to annotate each `Put` with some arbitrary metadata, so we can implement interesting features based on that. Of course, Redis is a server instead of  a library, not casual for changing data format. But there may be several common requires that we can support, at least, we also can make "annotations" is legal in AOF, AOF tools could skip them if they don't want to parse them.

In current idea, the annotations doesn't fully break AOF format, just add some lines that starts with `#`, like some languages annotation, after `#`, we could add useful information which we want. The annotations are only text instead of binary safe, of course, there can be multi lines together to explain context much clearly.

The followings are several scenarios I think of.

- Restore from a specific point-in-time
   Users may ask us to provide one ability:  restore data from a specific point-in-time, but there is no time info even during writing AOF (rather than AOF rewrite). One idea is that add some timestamp in AOF, timestamp precision may be minute or second, to avoid making AOF over-inflated. If there are some timestamps, it is easy to restore from a specific point-in-time by replaying AOF to a certain point in timestamp.
    ```
    # timestamp
    SET A B
    SET B C
    # timestamp
    SET C D
    SET D E
    ```

- Keys eviction
    Redis sometimes evicts keys silently, especially before #7653, actually, sometimes we may want to know keys are evicted or deleted, and the reason why redis start to evict keys (we lose context forever after finishing eviction, moreover, since of eviction is blocking, we can't learn useful things by `INFO` command), so it is very useful to record these important infos if possible.
    ```
    # start to evict keys since of maxmemory is 10GB, but used memory is 11GB
    # overhead memory 500MB, dataset memory 8GB, ...
    # timestamp
    DEL A (RESP)
    DEL B (RESP)
    # end evicting keys
    ```

- PSYNC-AOF
   AFAIK, there is not only one company that implement PSYNC based on AOF,  antirez also opened an issue #4357 to discuss this topic, he also designed one kind of AOF annotations for implementing PSYNC based on AOF. Maybe we can record some commands' offset, after syncing several commands in AOF, and then force to reset replica's replication offset by the record replication offset in AOF (because the content of AOF is not the same as replication backlog). This feature may provide convenience for implementing PSYNC-AOF.
   ```
    # replication offset $offset
    SET A B
    SET C D
    ...
    # replication offset $offset
    EXPIRE A 10
    EXPIRE C 10
   ```
- Dangerous commands
   In production environments, for some dangerous command, we usually block them by `rename-command` or ACL rules, but if actually they are executed, we still want to know who did this operation, when it happened, maybe other things, and we may also want to get this information fo audit. Moreover, for `slowlog` that update database, we maybe could put the metrics of slow log around the write command, so we could see much more slow logs on disk instead of just only those on limited memory. Of course, we can record these in server log, but we always store these commands in AOF, so it is not costly, but this is worth arguing.
   ```
   # timestamp
   # host: 127.0.0.1
   # ACL user
   flushall
   flushdb
   ```

If you do secondary development based on Redis, maybe you can add more infos for your purpose, such as active-active geo-distribution,  audit log. Welcome to communicate!

Hello guys,

I faced a really bad problem with getting all data from millions of hash keys, each hash around 9 key/value.

In Python first I will need a chunk maker function to split list of hash keys
`def build_chunks(lst, n):`
`.....for i in range(0, len(lst), n):`

Example in the zrange_key is a list of 1,000,000 hash keys:

`.....chunk_pipline = client.pipeline()`
`.....chunk_pipline.multi()`

Hi, 

I would like to bounce an idea with the folks here. Let's say we have a cluster of 10 nodes with 5 masters and 5 slaves.  When one pair of master and slave are down and permanently removed from the cluster, we have certain slots not covered temporarily, which is fine. The slot assignment information however is available in the other nodes and can be learned by the new node. author: PingXie

title: Writable replicas: yes or no?
body:
TL;DR Since time immemorial, Redis has allowed stand-alone and cluster [replicas to be configured so they can accept write requests](https://redis.io/topics/replication#read-only-replica). If you have an opinion about this feature, please add your voice to this discussion.

The primary use of Redis replicas is to provide a highly-available database service via failover and promotion. Replicas can also be used to offload reads from the master. However, a client can write to a replica under certain conditions (with the proper configuration and/or connection settings).

The motivations for making replicas writable, as far as we're aware, were mainly to support these use cases:

a. Allow creating (and possibly deleting) temporary keys, such as those that `ZUNIONSTORE` produces
b. Allow using commands that have the potential to write to keys, even if they don't necessarily do so, such as with using `SORT` in its read-only invocation form.

However, with Redis v6.2 and the upcoming v7, a slew of new `_RO` commands and complementary non-`STORE` variants have been added to address just that.

If that's indeed the case, namely that writable replicas are no longer really needed, the next question is whether they are needed at all. Supporting write replicas not only adds to the overall complexity of the project but also introduces several edge cases that, while rare, have damage potential during runtime. While the effort can be invested to address some/all of the issues, we're looking to assess the need and requirements from the feature.

So the questions we are looking to answer are mainly:

1. Are you using/have used Redis' writable replicas? If yes, what is/was the use case?
2. If you've answered yes to the above, are you writing to keys that also exist on the master?
3. And, if yes is your answer to the first question, are the keys written to the replica set with a TTL so they'll expire?

Thanks in advance for your participation!

title: Contribution Guidelines
body:
This page describes the process we apply for managing issues: bug reports, fixes, improvements, feature requests, and other ideas that may end up as part of the Redis project.

Redis is an open-source, community-oriented project, so it's open for community members to contribute and influence it. There are many ways an individual can contribute:
* Report a bug or limitation
* Suggest a new feature or improvement
* Engage in an ongoing discussion and provide insight based on the current experience using Redis
* Provide a pull request that solves a problem or offers an improvement or new feature
* Review a pull request made by another community member
* Suggest documentation corrections or improvements
* Help other community members by answering posted questions or assisting in troubleshooting and solving a problem

A @redis/core-team of five members drives the Redis project following the [project governance](https://redis.io/docs/about/governance/) structure. Running the project is a massive undertaking, and we rely on two things to succeed:
1. A structured process for triaging and managing issues and pull requests.
2. A Redis-contributors team: individuals whose familiarity and long-term commitment to the project are above average.

# What do Redis-contributors do

There are many forms of contribution, including:

* Assist in grooming the issue backlog by identifying obsolete or duplicate issues, labeling according to project guidelines, etc.
* Respond and answer new issues
* Perform code review
* Participate in and contribute to discussions
* Investigate bug reports and other issues, and file new pull requests to solve them
* Implement features and capabilities on the roadmap
* Monitor CI and investigate failures

We want to emphasize that we welcome this kind of contribution from all community members, not strictly Redis contributors.

Nominated Redis contributors have additional triage permissions, so they can perform more operations such as labeling or closing issues and pull requests.

# Guidelines for Redis contributors

These guidelines are provided here mainly for contributors but can also help other non-contributor members of the community better understand our process.

## General

If you're unsure about the implications or history of something, feel free to consult other contributors or the core team via a mention in GitHub or Slack. Start by **`@mentioning`** one person, and include others only if it becomes necessary.

Most of our work is around collaboration and gets done on GitHub using issues and pull requests. Below, you can learn more about how we use the platform.

## Issue Assignment

We use issue assignment in two ways:

* Ask someone to take ownership and work on an issue.
* Indicate someone is working on an issue to avoid having different people working on the same thing.

The rules are:

* Feel free to assign an issue to yourself if you want, and you can take it in a reasonable time frame.
* Feel free to assign the issue to someone else if you think that person can handle it.
* Feel free to un-assign yourself, even if assigned by someone else, if you're unable or don't have the time to handle an issue.

Assignments should be current and up to date and relate to the near future. Because of that, we don't assign most of the work in the backlog.

## Labels

We label issues and pull requests to track them quickly and efficiently and indicate what needs to be done to progress.

### Filter Labels

Because we work asynchronously, a big concern involves issues falling between the cracks. Many labels denote the current state of an issue so that we can effectively filter and find it later.

We usually don't clear labels when done working or closing an issue.

The following are the primary labels we use. Some older issues may also have other labels which are now obsolete.

| Label | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `state:to-be-closed` | No more work is required, and the issue should be closed unless discussed further. |
| `state:major-decision` | Pull request represents a major decision, as defined in the project governance. Requires a majority (and ideally complete consensus) of the core team to approve. |
| `state:help-wanted` | Needs more work and may be suitable for random community members. |
| `approval-needed` | A major-decision pull request that is ready and awaits core team approval. |
| `release-notes` | The release notes should mention this change. |
| `breaking-change` | A potentially breaking change. |
| `interface-change` | Changes or extends the user interface (e.g., commands, arguments, configuration parameters, etc.). |

### State labels

These labels indicate the current state of the issue or pull request and what needs to be done to make progress.

| Label | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `state:needs-design` | Non-trivial implementation, requires design. |
| `state:needs-coding` | Ready for implementation, or requires more implementation. |
| `state:needs-test-code` | The pull request needs more tests to be coded. |
| `state:needs-testing` | Additional (manual) testing is required. |
| `state:needs-review` | Additional code review is required. |
| `state:needs-code-doc` | More or improvement to code documentation (comments) is required. |
| `state:needs-doc-pr` | This pull request introduces changes that require documentation changes, done as a separate pull request to the `redis-doc` repository |
| `state:needs-investigation` | The problem or solution is unclear. Some investigation is needed. |

For closed issues or pull requests, the following labels provide information about why they were closed:

* `status:wontfix`  
* `status:invalid`
* `status:unreproducible`
* `status:duplicate`

## Pull request's commits, top comment, and merging

We aim for the PR top comment to represent a comprehensive list of changes, implications, side effects, design consideration, refactoring and other unrelated changes, as well as any other important information that can be useful instead of reading the actual changes.
For bug fixes, it is important to state the scenario which leads to the bug, and the implication on when it happens.
We usually aim to merge PRs with a squash merge, creating one commit in the target branch, and use the PR top comment as the commit comment for the squash commit.

Because of this squash merge strategy, it is often preferred to avoid amending commits and force-pushing, and instead keep adding incremental changes as separate commits, this makes it easier to review.

There are cases where we'd like to avoid using the squash merge:
1. On PRs that have several distinct topics, each standing for itself in a separate commit, we can just merge these with a rebase merge.
2. On PRs that contain massive refactoring, we usually ask for the renames and code relocation to be done in separate commits from the actual changes (these commit don't actually stand for themselves or pass compilation), for these PRs we'll use a normal merge, creating a merge commit and posting the top comment as the merge commit's commit comment.

On PRs that are marked with `release-notes`, specifically ones with a lot of details and a long top comment, we would also like a section in the to comment containing a short release note statement (or statements if there are several of them)

## Branching and Release Strategy

Work is generally committed to the `unstable` branch, which is the base for the [major or minor releases](https://redis.io/docs/about/releases/).
When work on a release is ready, we fork a release branch from `unstable` and use it to create release candidates. At this time, we focus work on the upcoming release, so all commits to `unstable` naturally get merged to the release branch as well.
We continue to do so until we release the general availability version. After we feel the version is stable, typically after several bugfix releases, we unfreeze `unstable`, which receives commits intended for the next major or minor release.

## Projects

We list issues and pull requests in GitHub [projects](https://github.com/orgs/redis/projects) as part of work and release planning, and in order to track bugfixes that need to be backported.

| Project | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `Triage` | Incoming issues and pull requests that require more work to sort out, and not identified as critical or urgent. |
| Release `x.y` | Content for a specific upcoming major or minor release. |
| `x.y Backport` | Content to be backported for a particular upcoming bugfix release. |
| `Backlog` | Content that is planned but not yet scheduled for a release. |

Issues and pull requests are associated with a project when we plan or consider including them in a release.

New requests or ideas go through a preliminary evaluation. Quick or minor improvements are placed in the Triage project for further analysis. Larger or more complex topics are placed in Backlog or a specific release.

The Backlog project has a lot of extra information for each item, including:
* Category
* Priority
* Size
* Design stage

To preserve this information, backlog issues that get pulled into a specific release are *also* left in the backlog.

## Milestones

We use milestones to quickly and easily classify the possible timeframe for an issue or pull request:

| Milestone | Timeframe |
| --- | --- |
| `Next Minor backlog` | Features or changes too big for a bugfix release but small enough, so they don't defer to a major release. |
| `Next Major backlog` | Features that are big, complex, or introduce a significant breaking change that warrants a major release. |

These are obsolete and will be merged into the backlog project soon.

# Process overview

> ❗ This is still work in progress.

## Bug Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  new[New bug found] --> hasfix{Can provide a trivial fix?}
  hasfix -->|Yes| new-pr[Submit a PR]
  hasfix -->|No| new-issue[File an issue]
  new-issue --> triage[Triage]
  triage --> new-pr
  new-pr --> label-pr[Apply PR labels to express impact]
  label-pr --> semver-eligible{Eligible for a SemVer bugfix?}
  semver-eligible -->|Yes, or an exception| proj-sched[Add to release, backports projects]
  semver-eligible -->|No| backlog-sched[Add to backlog]
  proj-sched --> review[Review]
  review --> merge[Merge]
```

# How to help

## Helping with issue handling

**Is the issue labeled correctly?** If not, fix the labels.

**Does the issue involve a question?** If you can provide an answer, go ahead and reply. If the answer is trivial and it's not likely that it will turn into a discussion, you can also apply the "to-be-closed" label, or directly close it if you're sure about it.

**Does the issue describe a problem/bug report?** Even if you're not going to deep dive into it yourself (e.g., no time or experience with the specific issue), consider if the issue includes all the necessary details. If not, ask the original poster to provide it.

## Helping with pull request handling

**Does the pull request include complete information?** Does it describe the context, the problem it aims to solve, what feature it provides and for what use case, etc.? If not, ask the author to provide this information.

**Perform a code review**. Your code review may be valuable even if you're unfamiliar with the specific area of the code in question. Code review is an iterative process, and different emphasis is required depending on what stage it is in:
* Implementation details are less critical when conceptual issues are still unresolved.
* Minor styling feedback is less important if the implementation is incomplete or incorrect.

In many cases, even a partial review that results with *"Concept looks good to me, did not review the code itself"* is helpful.

**Consider the pull request completeness and quality:**
* Does it include all necessary tests? If not, ask the author to include that.
* Does it require documentation updates? If not, ask the author or at least apply the `doc-needed` label.
* Does the top comment reflect all the changes, their implications, and the scenarios they affect? If not, ask the author to improve, or in some cases, edit the top comment or title yourself.

## Closing issues

We aim to have the bottom comment(s) of closed issues tell the story of why the issue is closed. If that's not the case, consider adding a final note indicating the reason for closing (duplicate of another issue, fixed by another issue, etc.).

If not sure about closing an issue, use the `to-be-closed` label to indicate it should be closed after further review.

## Closing Duplicate Issues

Since there's no way to link issues as related or duplicate in GitHub, only [link Issues](https://docs.github.com/en/github/managing-your-work-on-github/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue) to PRs, and add a cross-reference in a comment. 

There are many duplicate reports, and part of our work in maintaining the repository is to sort them out.

Sometimes closing duplicates is not enough, and people often add more comments to an already closed issue.

To prevent that, we will add a bottom comment saying *"This issue is closed. Please continue the discussion in issue #1234"*.

title: How does the "unlink" command in Redis work?
body:
https://redis.io/commands/unlink/#deleting-keys-in-the-background

```
the command just unlinks the keys from the keyspace. The actual removal will happen later asynchronously.
```

According to the documentation, the Redis "unlink" command is understood to synchronously remove the key from the keyspace and then asynchronously remove the corresponding value in the background.

However, in some cases, values that have been unlinked using the "unlink" command are still returned in response to a "get" command within 10ms of the unlink command being executed.

Is it possible that in Redis, "unlink" works by asynchronously passing both the key and value to background tasks and immediately responding?

title: How to find JSON entries by filtering an array of strings using regex :) ?
body:
Hello,

Redis stack Docker container: `redis/redis-stack:latest`

Given the JSON value below, I'd like find all products that match a tag regex.
```
{
  "catalog": [
    {
      "name": "Product #1",
      "tags": [
        "LOCAL"
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "Product #2",
      "tags": [
        "LOCAL",
        "FAIR_TRADE"
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "Product #3",
      "tags": [
        "NOT_AVAILABLE",
        "FAIR_TRADE"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Command to create the entry:
`JSON.SET store $ '{"catalog":[{"name":"Product #1","tags":["LOCAL"]},{"name":"Product #2","tags":["LOCAL","FAIR_TRADE"]},{"name":"Product #3","tags":["NOT_AVAILABLE","FAIR_TRADE"]}]}'`

Searching product 3 using regex works fine:
`JSON.GET store "$.catalog[?(@.name =~ '(?i)3')]"`
gives
`"[{\"name\":\"Product #3\",\"tags\":[\"NOT_AVAILABLE\",\"FAIR_TRADE\"]}]""`

Then, check if product 3 has a tag containing the letter `r`:
`JSON.GET store "$.catalog[?((@.name =~ '(?i)3') && (@.tags[?(@ =~ '(?i)r')]))]"`
gives
`"[{\"name\":\"Product #3\",\"tags\":[\"NOT_AVAILABLE\",\"FAIR_TRADE\"]}]"`

Then, check if product 3 has a tag containing the letter `a`:
`JSON.GET store "$.catalog[?((@.name =~ '(?i)3') && (@.tags[?(@ =~ '(?i)a')]))]"`
gives
`"[]"`

I don't expect such result because Product #3 has 2 tags that contain the letter `a` !

Does someone faced such case ?
How to get the proper result ?

Additional test: operator `==` on tags works as expected:
`JSON.GET store "$.catalog[?((@.name =~ '(?i)3') && (@.tags[?(@ == 'FAIR_TRADE\')]))]"` and `JSON.GET store "$.catalog[?((@.name =~ '(?i)3') && (@.tags[?(@ == 'NOT_AVAILABLE')]))]"` give the correct result.

Thanks for your help.
Stephane

title: commandstats client report methods
body:
The INFO commandstats reports the client command `cmd_client` this covers all the `CLIENT` calls.  Far be it for me to suggestion that additional cardinality be added to the already TOO MUCH CARDINALITY metric space.  However I think it would be beneficial to extend to the commandstats functionality to also track each `CLIENT` method as well.

Similar to how the commandstats for the `TS` methods is handled e.g. `cmdstat_ts.get`, 
`cmdstat_ts.add`, `cmdstat_ts.range`, etc.

Something like:
```
cmdstat_client:calls=13909573,usec=389054744,usec_per_call=27.97,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_client.setinfo:calls=13909573,usec=389054744,usec_per_call=27.97,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_client.getinfo:calls=0,usec=389054744,usec_per_call=27.97,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_client.id:calls=0,usec=389054744,usec_per_call=27.97,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
# etc
```

I think that this could be beneficial at a deep level in helping to debug when and what method in a `CLIENT` calls fail, e.g. `CLIENT SETINFO`.  However arguably `cmdstat_client` would only count a failed_call if the entire `CLIENT` fails rather than reporting a fail if only one method fails but the `CLIENT` command ultimately succeeds, leaving the count of each method to record whether the `CLIENT <METHOD>` fails.

title: Redis re-hashes occurring at 3Gi Memory Usage. Why?
body:
👋🏻 Hey all, I'm trying to optimize the performance of one of our caches.

Some background, I've been working with vyaramaka, who wrote [this issue](https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/12602).

TL;DR on that issue is that our caches are pretty big (like 30-50M keys each on 20-ish instances) and we hit a failure mode where Redis wants to re-hash at 4Gi of memory usage. Problem is that we use TTL on all values in the cache, and so the workload of expiring keys + serving requests + a rehash = Redis is pegged for minutes at a time.

To avoid that problem, we figured switching to primarily an LRU cache, and not setting a TTL on most keys would lighten the workload on Redis and eliminate or at least reduce the problem.

Good news is that we have seen improvements! Re-hashes no longer peg the CPU.

![Screenshot 2024-01-18 at 10 28 08](https://github.com/redis/redis/assets/42927786/2ded143e-ebe2-4433-a587-03da8421ca62)
![Screenshot 2024-01-18 at 10 28 30](https://github.com/redis/redis/assets/42927786/5799e05c-263b-460f-be42-af8ef2c83241)

But, that brings me to my question: **We noticed that with this setup, the rehashes occur at 3Gi instead of 4Gi, and in fact, re-hashes won't occur after that up to 7Gi. Why???** 

We took a look at the # of keys in the cache for both our vanilla setup and this new "Selective TTL" setup as I'm calling it, and when the re-hashes occur, the number of keys is 33.54M for vanilla, and 33.17M for Selective TTL (roughly(tm) the same)

I've been able to reproduce this result 100% of the time (again, good news!), so I think there's just some machination of Redis that I don't understand. I thought that re-hashing might have been controlled by the amount of memory that the internal hash table was using, but is it instead amount of keys?

If anyone knows, I'd really appreciate an answer to this riddle. Thank you! 🙇🏻

title: Correction Needed in Redis Documentation - Most Recently Used (MRU)
body:
Noticed a discrepancy in the documentation (linked below) regarding MRU cache policy. It's a minor thing, just wanted to get it corrected.

It currently states: "Most Recently Used (MRU), which prioritizes the _**removal**_ of the most recently accessed data." However, based on my understanding of cache policies, there may be a typographical error in this statement.

The correct behaviour of the MRU cache policy should prioritize the _**retention**_ of the most recently accessed data, not its removal.

_Source: https://redis.com/glossary/cache-memory/#:~:text=Cache%20memory%20is%20typically%20divided,has%20varying%20sizes%20and%20speeds._

## Error in: 

"The decision-making process regarding which data to retain in the cache and which to discard is governed by a cache policy. Common policies include Least Recently Used (LRU), which discards the data that has remained unused for the longest duration, and Most Recently Used (MRU), which prioritizes the removal of the most recently accessed data."

## Change it to:

"The decision-making process regarding which data to retain in the cache and which to discard is governed by a cache policy. Common policies include Least Recently Used (LRU), which discards the data that has remained unused for the longest duration, and Most Recently Used (MRU), which prioritizes the retention of the most recently accessed data."

----

Apologies if I'm in the wrong discussion group. Just wanted to bring this tiny thing to attention.

title: Copy entire contents of one virtual db to another one inside same Redis instance, without using backup utilities
body:
I inherited a system that was designed and implemented by a web developer, when it's not really a web application.  I'm stuck with it.  

The simplest way I can think of to solve the current problem I'm facing involves keeping "snapshots" of the contents of one virtual DB at three points in time, overwriting in a FIFO daisy-chain.   I've spent many hours looking for a way to accomplish this, but unfortunately search results are dominated by backup and recovery solutions, which is not what I need.  

There's not a lot of data; like, it would be measured in megabytes, maybe four or so.  Nothing, by DB or caching standards.  But I need to take these point-in-time snapshots frequently; more than twice a minute.  I mean, that's not frequently by many standards, but it does preclude any solution that involves running some command line tool or going through some backup and restoration process.  It's not going to be all that uncommon to restore from one of the two non-current copies-- they're definitely not for disaster recovery purposes.

I can sort of understand why functionality like this wouldn't be in much demand for a caching layer, because it's so non-performant, and the data is presumably changing while you're copying.  But our system has regular periods of times, lasting multiple seconds, when no data should be getting changed; my plan is to use those regularly scheduled periods of cache inactivity to make the copy.  

So I want to copy the entire contents (all whopping 4mb or so) from one virtual data base to another, in code.  Python if possible. 
 I thought as a last resort, surely I could just iterate through all the keys and copy them (and their values) by first bringing them into my applications memory, then just writing them out.  But even that seems to be very challenging, as there is apparently no programmatic way to iterate through all the keys in the given virtual DB.  If it makes a difference, the way I'm currently connecting to Redis is through Django's django.core.cache object, but I could connect another way for this purpose if necessary.

As my deadline is measured in days, not weeks, any solution that involves changing the basic architecture-- like "hey, it's only 4mb, you don't need Redis, dummy!"-- just isn't going to be practical.  If I do a good job with this, I hope to get the opportunity to re-architect if from an application programmer's perspective, rather than a web designer's; but I don't have much time to prove myself.  Any pointers or suggestions gratefully accepted.  Thanks!
author: andrewbgross

title: Managing Streams memory on high volatility scenarios
body:
Hi guys, first time writing here, hope to get some light shed in my problem.

We're using Redis Streams to serve as a short-living storage in a micro-service, but the memory consumption is going through the roof very fast. The scenario is:

1. Receive an http call, XAdd the data to the stream, finish.
2. On multiple micro-service instances (each one is a different consumer), do a XReadGroup on that stream. After working with the messages data, we XAck it.
3. In a best case scenario, the data should live in the stream for a couple of seconds.

But even so the memory usage increases very fast, XTrim won't help much since we can't afford to lose unread messages. **I tried to do an XDel on the messages after the XAck, but the command always returns 0.**

### Questions:

- Does XAck not only removes the message from the PEL, but deletes the record from the stream?
  - If so, why the memory consumption keeps rising?
  - If not, why XDel returns 0?
- Should I do XDel and then XAck?

Any suggestions would be very welcoming, thanks!

title: How is the memory usage for the key-value calculated?
body:
I encountered an issue when setting keys with similar values in my Redis environment (version 7.0). Specifically, I ran the following commands:

```shell
127.0.0.1:6379> set aaaaaa abcdef
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> set aaaaaaa abcdef
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> memory usage aaaaaa
(integer) 64
127.0.0.1:6379> memory usage aaaaaaa
(integer) 72
```

This led me to the following questions:

1. Why does the memory usage increase to 72 bytes when I only add one additional character to the key?
2. How is the memory usage for the key `aaaaaa` calculated?

I attempted to calculate it myself using the following logic:

- **Key (`aaaaaa`)**: 
  - Redis Object Metadata: 16 bytes
  - Length of Key: 1 byte
  - Allocation Size: 1 byte
  - Flags: 1 byte
  - Key Value: 6 bytes (`abcdef`)
  - Null Terminator: 1 byte
  - Total: 26 bytes

- **Value (`abcdef`)**:
  - Redis Object Metadata: 16 bytes
  - Length of Value: 1 byte
  - Allocation Size: 1 byte
  - Flags: 1 byte
  - Value: 6 bytes (`abcdef`)
  - Null Terminator: 1 byte
  - Total: 26 bytes

- **Dictionary Entry**:
  - Pointer to Key: 8 bytes
  - Pointer to Value: 8 bytes
  - Next: 8 bytes
  - Total: 24 bytes

However, even with these calculations, the total memory usage exceeds 64 bytes. Could you help me understand where I might be going wrong?

---

Feel free to ask if you need further clarification or have any additional questions!

title: Concurrent Redis SCAN
body:
# Proposal for Enhancing Redis SCAN for Concurrent Operations

## Background

The current cursor-based mechanism of Redis's `SCAN` command presents challenges for concurrent operations, particularly in scenarios where Redis is hosted remotely or efficient pagination is needed.

## Problem Statement

The existing `SCAN` operation is sequential and dependent on a server-generated cursor. When attempting to concurrently fetch keys matching a pattern, tasks frequently share the same cursor since the updated cursor value is unavailable until the preceding `SCAN` call completes. This limits the ability to fully exploit concurrent operations, resulting in reduced performance and scalability, and inefficient utilization of Async I/O capabilities.

## Proposed Enhancements

1. **Manual Cursor Management**
   - Introduce an optional parameter in the `SCAN` command to allow users to provide and increment the cursor manually.
   - This would enable clients to independently manage cursor state across concurrent tasks, bypassing the blocking nature of the `SCAN` response.

2. **Simplify Cursor Type**
   - Currently, the cursor is returned as a string, adding unnecessary overhead when handling it programmatically.
   - Returning it as an integer or providing a configuration option to toggle between types would enhance usability.

## Benefits

- **Improved Performance**: Manual cursor management facilitates true parallelism by enabling independent tasks to proceed without waiting for a shared cursor update.
- **Enhanced Usability**: Simplifying the cursor type and providing flexibility in its management reduces development overhead and improves integration with Async I/O frameworks.
- **Backward Compatibility**: These changes can be implemented as optional enhancements, ensuring existing applications are unaffected.

## Example Use Case

Consider a method to erase user-specific cache keys using `SCAN` with a given pattern:

```ruby
def erase_user_cache(user_id)
  cursor = '0'
  barrier = Async::Barrier.new
  semaphore = Async::Semaphore.new(@config[:redis][:pool][:size])
  matched_keys = []

  loop do
    semaphore.acquire do
      barrier.async do
        cursor, keys = @redis_client.scan(cursor, match: "user:#{user_id}:", count: 1000)
        matched_keys += keys
      end
      break if cursor == '0'
    end
  end

  barrier.wait
  @redis_client.del(matched_keys) unless matched_keys.empty?
ensure
  barrier.stop
end
```

The issue here is that concurrent tasks often share the same cursor value because the Redis `SCAN` operation blocks until the cursor is updated, resulting in redundant scans and wasted resources.

title: Seeking Guidance for Upgrading from Redis Cluster 3.2 to 4.x or Later Versions
body:
In our production environment, we have been running Redis Cluster version 3.2 and are now considering an upgrade to Redis Cluster 4.x or a later stable version. However, given the significant changes between these versions, especially concerning the cluster bus protocol compatibility as mentioned in the official [4.0 RELEASE NOTES](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/antirez/redis/4.0/00-RELEASENOTES), I am seeking advice on the best practices and steps involved in executing this upgrade.

Specifically, the release notes indicate that "The Redis Cluster bus protocol of 4.0 is no longer compatible with Redis 3.2. This change was necessary to provide Docker/NAT compatibility for Redis Cluster. Therefore, upgrading a Redis Cluster to 4.0 requires a mass restart of all instances." In our current setup, such a mass restart would mean all instances would be simultaneously replaced and restarted, potentially causing significant disruption to our live services.

Therefore, I request guidance on the following points:

Is there a recommended step-by-step guide or checklist available to ensure a smooth transition from Redis Cluster 3.2 to 4.x or a later version?
Given that the incompatible cluster bus protocol necessitates a mass restart of all instances, are there alternative strategies—such as rolling upgrades—that can minimize downtime and reduce the impact on our live services? If not, what preparations or mitigation measures can we implement to ensure minimal disruption?
We highly value the expertise and experience within this community and greatly appreciate any guidance, recommendations, or personal experiences shared by those who have successfully completed this upgrade.

title: Red Lock Algorithm Rethinking
body:
In order to acquire the lock, the client performs the following operations:

1. It gets the current time in milliseconds.
2. It tries to acquire the lock in all the N instances sequentially, using the same key name and random value in all the instances. During step 2, when setting the lock in each instance, the client uses a timeout which is small compared to the total lock auto-release time in order to acquire it. For example if the auto-release time is 10 seconds, the timeout could be in the ~ 5-50 milliseconds range. This prevents the client from remaining blocked for a long time trying to talk with a Redis node which is down: if an instance is not available, we should try to talk with the next instance ASAP.
3. The client computes how much time elapsed in order to acquire the lock, by subtracting from the current time the timestamp obtained in step 1. If and only if the client was able to acquire the lock in the majority of the instances (at least 3), and the total time elapsed to acquire the lock is less than lock validity time, the lock is considered to be acquired.
4. If the lock was acquired, its validity time is considered to be the initial validity time minus the time elapsed, as computed in step 3.
5. If the client failed to acquire the lock for some reason (either it was not able to lock N/2+1 instances or the validity time is negative), it will try to unlock all the instances (even the instances it believed it was not able to lock).

**The above five steps are how we should do to acquire a red lock. As what I know, we need to acquire all the N instances sequentially to avoid the dead lock. If we just want to avoid the dead lock, we could acquire the first N/2 locks sequentially, and we could get the last locks simultaneously. Because we have get the first N/2 locks, then if we could get one lock again, then we could get the red lock.**

It is nice for you to give me some opinions about this. And welcome to talk about it.

title: Rethinking the leader election process
body:
We know that the current leader election is as following: https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/reference/cluster-spec/ (Replica election and promotion). I have an idea about this stage, but I don't make sure whether I miss something or not. And I would give the idea in the following:
**Masters reply to replica vote request**
1. A replica would send the election request to the master with epoch, and **a random number**. And if other conditions is same, we think the replica with a bigger random number have a higher priority.
2. A master only votes a single time for a given epoch, and refuses to vote for older epochs: every master has a lastVoteEpoch field and will refuse to vote again as long as the currentEpoch in the auth request packet is not greater than the lastVoteEpoch. When a master replies positively to a vote request, the lastVoteEpoch is updated accordingly, and safely stored on disk. But there is an exception. If a master vote for a replica, but the replica send a message to a master that the replica give up the election for currentEpoch, then the master could vote for another replica, which with a higher priority.
3. When a replica send a election request to a master, and the master have voted. The master would tell it which replica gets its vote. If a replica have found that more than half of the master nodes have voted to other replicas and there are some replicas with higher priority. The replica would send messages to all the masters, who vote for the replica and tell them the replica give up the election for currentEpoch, and tells them the replica with the highest number, who also want to win the election, then these master would vote for the highest priority replica. 
4. The masters, who receive the give up message, would compare the priority that it receives from the give up replica with the replica election requests they receive. And then these masters would vote for the replicas with highest priority again. 
5. The replica, who receives the vote for more than one half of masters will win the election.
6. A master votes for a replica only if the replica's master is flagged as FAIL.
7. Auth requests with a currentEpoch that is less than the master currentEpoch are ignored. Because of this the master reply will always have the same currentEpoch as the auth request. If the same replica asks again to be voted, incrementing the currentEpoch, it is guaranteed that an old delayed reply from the master can not be accepted for the new vote.


Thanks for the opinions about the ideas before.

title: Redis multi-tiered caches: is "cache" the right word in such configurations?
body:
I have a question regarding how (or if) tiered Redis caches can be configured, and what the word "cache" means. I have done some searching and LLM-summary reading, but this is a keyword-dense question and I found no suitable answers.

I'm coming from the world of DNS caches and web caches, so apologies if my nomenclature is not consistent.

Redis at higher levels is fairly new to me, though I have been using trivial Redis instances in the past for many years. I have an application that requires a layered "cache" model. By this I mean that an application sends a query to a local Redis instance, for a SET query. The SET query is pointed at a fairly large number of objects in the set - anywhere from a few dozen to a few million. There are thousands (or tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands!) of SETs as this will grow in scale.

I have:
  - limited memory on the edge nodes, such that I cannot store all SETs in every distributed cache (not enough memory)
  - small numbers of users who are only interested in a small sub-section of the full list of SETs that exist (I don't need all SETs in all locations)
  - very very fast access required for answers for SISMEMBER SET queries (<.1ms or less)
  - no way to tell what the needs are at any site until the actual questions are being asked to Redis (highly diverse and non-predictable data access)
  -  a strong interest in using a single API (Redis) for all parts of this system, instead of customizing my own code to provide efficiency
 
I'm wondering if there has ever been any consideration of doing partial replication between Redis instances based on query patterns, not as a universal duplication of all data. This would look similar to how DNS caches work today: a request for an object comes in, the local cache is examined.  If no answer exists in cache, then the singular query is sent onwards to (probably) another cache. If it does not have the answer, it sends onwards to other caches or to authoritative servers (this is only one diagram of many possible layerings of DNS caches; let's use it for this discussion.)  Only what is needed is stored, by all members in the query path.

What I'm missing in my understanding of the Redis model is that there seems to be no "cache" feature between Redis instances - there is only "replicate," and "replicate" implies 100% of the data from one primary server, transmitted to the subsidiary servers. This seems highly inefficient.  Why not just wait until there is a query at the edge node, then relay that to the central system, which would then reply (possibly with a "fast response" of that exact question) and then which would start replicating the data required to provide that answer?  In this way the edge systems would have only and exactly what was required for their needs: Redis instances at the edge of the diagram would only have exactly as much data as they needed to answer for the clients connecting to them. It could be possible for the replication to have a TTL, such that the primary server would keep sending data updates to the subsidiary edge server until a timer expired, and then the cached data in the edge server would be deleted, the replication would stop, and resources would be preserved only for actively used data that required replication. The downside is that the first instances of queries to a SET might be a bit slow as the initial queries would be to an empty cache set, or would be answered by the central Redis instance before the full replication became available to the edge node. This may be acceptable, or may be mostly mitigated by some priming queries - that is a minor detail for application-layer implementation.

Again: my concept of "cache" perhaps is different. A DNS server does not cache the entire DNS  - it only caches things that have been recently asked.  A web cache does not store the entire Internet - it just caches things that have been recently requested. Cannot this model work with Redis?

Note that this is slightly different than caching the answer to a query, which can be done in the application and outside of Redis. With very large SET queries, one would need to duplicate the underlying data that provides the answer (and keep it fresh and updated) versus just caching the answers that came from the queries pointed at the SET data.

I see how I could write some tool to mimic the Redis API and then shuffle data between Redis instances but ... that's terribly ugly when it seems that this should be a native Redis function and not some bodged-up glue code.

Is it possible to configure Redis in such a cascading, memory-sparse fashion?  Am I missing the obvious in the documentation? Do I need to forget the way the word "cache" has been used up until now in my experiences?

JT

title: Sentinel disconnection
body:
Sentinel Question:

We have a multi-zone Sentinel deployment in EKS, where 2 DB pods (node-mz-0 and 1) contain a redis process and a sentinel process, and a third pod (sentinel-mz-0) runs only a sentinel.
At some points in time, we experience unexplained failover events, and we cannot figure out what caused the "disconnection".
The deployment has TLS enabled for replication and client connections.
The nodes and sentinels communicate via a DNS endpoint pointed to a public IP address.

Here's the timeline of one of the recent events:
1. Sentinel Detection and Consensus (11:44:47 - 11:44:48)
11:44:47: The Sentinel on node-mz-0 is the first to detect that the master, node-mz-0, is subjectively down (+sdown).
11:44:48: The Sentinel on node-mz-1 also detects that the master is subjectively down (+sdown).
11:44:48: The Sentinels reach a consensus (#quorum 2/2 and then 3/2 is logged by sentinel-mz-0) that the master is objectively down (+odown).
11:44:48: The Sentinels elect sentinel-mz-0 to be the leader for the failover process.

2. Master Promotion (11:44:48)
11:44:48: The elected leader sends a REPLICAOF NO ONE command to node-mz-1.
11:44:48: node-mz-1 receives the command and immediately logs that it has been promoted to master mode. It also executes a CONFIG REWRITE to persist its new role.

3. Cluster Reconfiguration and Synchronization (11:44:49 - 11:45:11)

title: Why is filtering not done before KNN in FLAT index?
body:
Hi,
I'm using MemoryDB in AWS, with Redis 7.1.1 as the underlying engine

I've got a FLAT vector index with 400k vectors - the vectors are of 1024 dimensions.

I'm running hybrid searches in my app. I've got 1 Tag field that I use to filter the results.

In my vector index, I have two datasets, one of ~50k vectors, and one of 463 vectors, each associated with a specific owner TAG.
When I run a search query without filter this is what FT.PROFILE returns:
 [[b'sync.time', 9], [b'query.time', 247148], [b'vector.count', 10], [b'vector.time', 247143], [b'result.count', 10], [b'result.time', 0]]
 
When I run it with filtering on the 463:
 [[b'tag.count', 463], [b'sync.time', 1], [b'query.time', 846], [b'vector.count', 10], [b'vector.time', 843], [b'lowpass.count', 1], 'result.count', 10], [b'result.time', 0]]

When I run it with filtering on the 50k:
[[b'tag.count', 0], [b'sync.time', 2], [b'query.time', 367244], [b'vector.count', 10], [b'vector.time', 367240], [b'result.count', 10], b'result.time', 0]]

When filtering on the small set, it seems like filtering is done before the KNN, and therefore the low latency.
When filtering on the big set, it seems like filtering is not done before KNN, and the time it takes is significantly larger than without filtering at all.

I'd like to understand why the filter is not being applied before the KNN search, and causing a massive spike in query time.
Accuracy is very important for me, so I'm reluctant to move to HNSW index.
Is there anything I can do, besides moving to HNSW index?

title: the info `maxmemory_policy:volatile-lru` `maxmemory_human:20.00G` and `evicted_keys:110895298`, but why the `used_memory_peak_human:12.93G` is less than `maxmemory_human:20.00G`
body:
my redis-server is running in a Docker container,  the basic info is as follows:

The redis-server version: 5.0.3
The available memory of the container is 24G. (get 25769803776 via command `head /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes`).
The max usaged memory of the container is 24G. (get 25769803776 via command `head /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.max_usage_in_bytes`).

### Some `redis info` is as follows:

Get `maxmemory_human:20.00G` and `maxmemory_policy:volatile-lru` via command `info memory`, this means the evication is enabled.
Get `evicted_keys:110895298` via command `info stats`, this means some keys have indeed been evicted.

But the `used_memory_peak_human:12.93G` is less than `maxmemory_human:20.00G`.

### The implementation of these statistical metrics in the code:

`used_memory_peak` update by a timer function `serverCron`, it execute once every 100 ms.

https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/b4867130f40e2df366b740e118405187608856ae/src/server.c#L1140-L1141

When executing a command, the `freeMemoryIfNeeded` method is invoked in the `processCommand` method to evict memory.

https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/b4867130f40e2df366b740e118405187608856ae/src/evict.c#L460-L466

He will first determine whether memory eviction is needed by calling the `getMaxmemoryState` method.

https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/b4867130f40e2df366b740e118405187608856ae/src/evict.c#L401-L406

If some keys get deleted via memory eviction, increment the counter metric `server.stat_evictedkeys` here.

https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/b4867130f40e2df366b740e118405187608856ae/src/evict.c#L567-L576


I think that when evicted_keys > 0, used_memory_peak should also be greater than maxmemory. Is it right?
author: fantiq

title: Using UNLINK instead of DEL in the MIGRATE command
body:
As you might know Redis already provides config knobs to replace DEL with UNLINK in different situations like eviction, expiration and user delete.

Key migration (MIGRATE) is also using DEL internally to delete a key after copying it to the destination node:

"The command internally uses [DUMP](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/dump/) to generate the serialized version of the key value, and [RESTORE](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/restore/) in order to synthesize the key in the target instance. The source instance acts as a client for the target instance. If the target instance returns OK to the [RESTORE](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/restore/) command, the source instance deletes the key using [DEL](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/del/)."

My question for the community is that if you see any downsides in replacing DEL with UNLINK in the key migration function. In other words, is there a reason that there is no config knob for this particular DEL use case.

title: What's the recommended best practice for handling SUBSCRIBE commands in RESP3 clients?
body:
Hi all,

After having read [this issue](https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/11784), it's still not clear to me what is the recommended way of handling SUBSCRIBE commands in client libraries that perform automatic pipelining of commands.

Context: I co-maintain Boost.Redis. It exposes a `connection` type that only supports RESP3, automatically batches user requests and allows regular requests to be mixed with PubSub flow. There is a request queue, and responses are matched to requests by order. Pushes are extracted and handled in a separate channel.

At the moment, SUBSCRIBE is considered to have no response. SUBSCRIBE triggers a RESP3 push (`'>'`) for each channel that the user subscribed to. We just consider SUBSCRIBE to have no response, and place these pushes in the notification channel. So far, so good.

I've recently found out that Redis might reject subscriptions due to insufficient ACL permissions. If this is the case, then SUBSCRIBE does have a regular response (`-ERR: whatever`). The problem here is our current approach breaks (with potential security implications) when these kind of errors are received. They will be matched to the next request, causing the pipeline to go "out of sync". So I'm trying to find out a solution.

My idea is to try to figure out how many pushes each (P)SUBSCRIBE/(P)UNSUBSCRIBE expect, then wait for them as if they are regular request/response messages. This requires inspecting the push first field to dispatch it to either the push handler or not.
Is what I'm saying wise? Is it guaranteed that these confirmation pushes will arrive before the responses to commands issued after the (P)(UN)SUBSCRIBE? Is there a better way to implement this?

Thanks.

author: Branhub

title: 1bench — native Redis GUI
body:
Hey Redis community,

Built [1bench](https://1bench.dev/redis) — a native desktop GUI for Redis.

Redis-specific:
- Purpose-built 2-panel key browser — namespace tree on the left, key details on the right, tree or flat view, keyspace search
- Type-aware editors — strings, hashes as tables with fields/values/row numbers, lists with indices, sets with members, sorted sets with scores, streams with recent entries
- Server Overview — version, mode (standalone/cluster/sentinel), uptime, memory and peak, ops/sec, hit rate, evictions, connected clients, replica status, per-database key counts (most Redis GUIs skip this)
- TTL inspection and editing per key, bulk delete, rename
- Command console with raw CLI mode or a visual builder (GET/SET/DEL, HGET/HSET/HGETALL, LPUSH/LRANGE, SMEMBERS, TTL/EXPIRE, KEYS/SCAN)
- Command history per connection, searchable and re-runnable; pin favorites
- Batch-commit edits — stage changes across keys, commit together
- Works with Redis Cloud, AWS ElastiCache, Azure Cache for Redis, and self-hosted
- SSH tunnel support for private Redis instances

Also works with Valkey, Dragonfly, KeyDB, DiceDB, and Kvrocks — same RESP-oriented workflow, no relearning.

It also supports Postgres, Elasticsearch, ClickHouse, Qdrant, and more if you run a multi-DB stack — but the Redis experience is built native, not a SQL-first tool retrofitted with a key browser.

100% local, zero telemetry, direct connection (no proxy).

Feedback welcome — especially on what feels missing or awkward in your Redis GUI workflow.

title: Wingfoil — a Rust stream-processing graph framework with a Redis adapter
body:
Hi all,

Wanted to share something we recently shipped that builds on Redis, in case it's
useful to others here and to get any feedback on the integration choices.

[Wingfoil](https://github.com/wingfoil-io/wingfoil) is a Rust stream-processing
library — you wire up a graph of nodes where each node ticks when its upstreams
produce a value, and the graph runs either in real time or replayed from
historical data. It's aimed at high-frequency trading and real-time AI pipelines.

We just added a Redis adapter that exposes Redis as wingfoil source and sink
nodes, covering **two transports**:

- **Pub/Sub** — `redis_sub` subscribes to a channel and emits each message into
  the graph; `redis_pub` publishes a stream of messages back out.
- **Streams** — `redis_stream_read` does a snapshot-then-tail read of a stream,
  and `redis_stream_write` appends via `XADD`.

A couple of design points we'd love eyes on:

- **Snapshot → tail handoff.** For streams we run `XRANGE key - +` to replay the
  backlog, capture the last entry ID, then `XREAD BLOCK 0 STREAMS key <last_id>`
  for the live tail. Because the tail reads strictly *after* the snapshot
  boundary ID, anything appended in the handoff window is delivered by `XREAD`
  (its ID is greater) and nothing is re-delivered. No missed or duplicated
  entries.
- **Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget.** No backlog/replay/offsets, so a subscriber
  only sees messages published after its `SUBSCRIBE` completes — we treat that as
  an explicit no-snapshot path rather than papering over it.
- Built on async connections (`tokio-comp`); the blocking `XREAD` tail runs on a
  dedicated connection so blocking it indefinitely is safe.

A concrete use case: fanning out a normalised market-data stream over Redis
Pub/Sub to a fleet of lightweight consumers, while persisting the same events to
a Redis Stream for replay/backtesting through wingfoil's historical run mode.

Links:
- Adapter source: https://github.com/wingfoil-io/wingfoil/tree/main/wingfoil/src/adapters/redis
- Wingfoil repo: https://github.com/wingfoil-io/wingfoil
- Project site: https://www.wingfoil.io/

Thanks for building Redis — happy to answer questions or dig into anything above.

We're actively looking for contributors, so if any of this is up your street
we'd love the help. And if wingfoil looks useful to you, a ⭐ on the
[repo](https://github.com/wingfoil-io/wingfoil) would mean a lot.

title: Security issues concerning logging
body:
Hello,

I am currently trying to understand some of the security aspects of Redis 7.2 (open source) and hope you can answer the following questions:

1) Does Redis include sensitive information in error messages facing end users (like usernames, passwords, sensitive data about internal state / production data)?
2) Does Redis log security-related events in such a way that they can be evaluated afterwards?
   For example, events like:
	- logins (also login attempts)
	- unauthorized operations (when an ACL user tries to perform a command which it is not allowed to perform)
	- runtime errors
	- changes of ACL permissions and passwords
	- changes to the Redis config and to the log settings
   If so, are ACL username, timestamp, performed operation, and status logged?
3) Does Redis log logins and operations performed by an ACL user, especially for "administrative" ACL users?
   If so, are ACL username, timestamp, and performed operation logged?
4) I hope you can clarify a question regarding the ACL log. Are those events logged at the logfile or only in some internal ringbuffer? The ACL log is limited in size and Redis is fast in processing, for example, user authentication attempts. I can periodically check the ACL log programmatically, but I think this would be prone to miss some events.

Thanks in advance
Uwe

title: Redis 8.10.2 has a dependency on Lua 5.1.5 which is an out of support library
body:
Hi everyone, 

The deps/README.md says, under Lua:

We use Lua 5.1 and no upgrade is planned currently, since we don't want to break Lua scripts for new Lua features: in the context of Redis Lua scripts the capabilities of 5.1 are usually more than enough, the release is rock solid, and we definitely don't want to break old scripts.

Two short questions from a downstream packager.

Is that still the position in 2026? We have to explain to reviewers why we ship Lua 5.1.5, which last shipped in February 2012. That README is the only statement we can point to and it carries no date. A maintainer confirming it still holds would settle it.

For deployments that never run scripts, is there a recommended way to disable scripting entirely? Not building the interpreter at all is [#13057](https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/13057), still open. Short of that, is there a configuration you would endorse and would consider documenting?
